As the Viking Age declined, the flow of Scandinavians to Rus' stopped and they gradually assimilated into Slavic culture by the late 11th century. Runestones in Sweden, such as the Greece Runestones, commemorate those who died abroad.
vardar: The Vardar is 388 kilometres long, of which 76 are in Greece, and drains an area of around 25,000 square kilometres. It rises at Vrutok, a few kilometres south-west of Gostivar in North Macedonia, and passes through Gostivar, Skopje and Veles. It crosses the Greek border near Gevgelija and flows by Polykastro and Axioupoli, meaning town on the Axios, before emptying into the Thermaic Gulf west of Thessaloniki. Its basin makes up two-thirds of the territory of North Macedonia. Its valley has fertile land in the Polog region, around Gevgelija and in the Thessaloniki regional unit, and mountains surround the river elsewhere.

The oldest known name of the river is Axios, mentioned by Homer as the home of the Paeonians, allies of Troy. The name Vardários was sometimes used by the ancient Greeks in the 3rd century BCE and widely in the Byzantine era, and the modern Vardar probably descends from it. The name may come from Thracian, though Dardanian, Paeonian, Ancient Macedonian and Greek were also spoken in the lands the river drains. Vardarios may derive from a Proto-Indo-European form meaning black water, and Axios may have meant dark or not shining. The Albanian author Pjetër Bogdani used the form Asi.

Under the Ottoman Empire the river became well known, and in Turkey it remains the inspiration for many folk songs, the best-known being Vardar Ovasi. It appears on the coat of arms of Skopje, which is part of the city's flag.

Together with the Loudias and the Haliacmon, the Vardar forms a large delta at the Axios-Loudias-Aliakmonas National Park. Greek National Road 1 and the M1 and E75 run within the valley along the river's length as far as near Skopje. A prevailing northerly ravine wind, the Vardaris or Vardarec, blows down the valley, usually as a breeze. When it meets the mountains between North Macedonia and Greece it gathers great momentum and brings cold conditions to Thessaloniki and the delta, especially in winter, when pressure over eastern Europe is higher than over the Aegean.
vasco-da-gama: Vasco da Gama was born in Sines, a seaport on the Alentejo coast of southwest Portugal. His father, Estêvão da Gama, had served as a knight of the household of Ferdinand, Duke of Viseu, rose in the ranks of the military Order of Santiago and was civil governor of Sines until 1478. Portuguese ships had worked down the African coast since the early 15th century, and Bartolomeu Dias had found the South Atlantic westerlies in 1487.

On 8 July 1497 da Gama left Lisbon with four ships and a crew of 170. After passing Sierra Leone he steered into the open ocean to catch the westerlies and made landfall on the African coast on 4 November 1497, having sailed more than 10,000 kilometres without touching land, the longest such journey made up to then. At Mozambique in March 1498 he posed as a Muslim to gain an audience with the sultan, but a hostile crowd drove him out. At Malindi a Gujarati pilot guided the fleet across the Indian Ocean.

The fleet anchored near Kozhikode on 20 May 1498. The Zamorin received da Gama, but the gifts were judged poor, Muslim merchants cast him as a pirate, and his request to leave a factor behind was turned down. The return crossing against the monsoon took more than 90 days, against 23 on the way out. Only about 55 men came home, and two ships were lost.

In 1502 da Gama commanded the fourth Portuguese India armada. Off Madayi he captured the pilgrim ship Mirim, which carried over 400 people, including about 50 women, and burned it with them aboard, according to the eyewitness Thomé Lopes and the chronicler Gaspar Correia. He then bombarded Kozhikode. Back in Portugal in September 1503, he was passed over when the first viceroy of India was named in 1505.

After Manuel I died in late 1521, King John III appointed da Gama governor of India, with the title of viceroy, in 1524. Da Gama contracted malaria soon after arriving and died in Cochin on 24 December 1524. His body was returned to Portugal in 1539. His voyage opened a sea route between Europe and India that the Portuguese held as a commercial monopoly for several decades. Luís de Camões wrote the national epic Os Lusíadas in his honour, while the killing of the pilgrims at sea has tempered his reputation.
vasco-nunez-de-balboa: Balboa was born in Jerez de los Caballeros, the third of four sons of the hidalgo Nuño Arias de Balboa. As a youth he served as a page and squire to Don Pedro de Portocarrero, lord of Moguer. In 1500 he sailed to the Americas on Rodrigo de Bastidas's expedition, which explored the Colombian coast and the Gulf of Urabá. He settled on Hispaniola in 1505 as a planter and pig farmer, ran into debt and in 1509 escaped his creditors by sailing as a stowaway, hidden in a barrel with his dog Leoncico, on the expedition of Martín Fernández de Enciso to Nueva Andalucía.

Balboa urged that the settlement of San Sebastián be moved to Darién, where the soil was more fertile. After a hard battle against the cacique Cémaco, the Spanish founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién in September 1510, keeping a vow to the Virgen de la Antigua. Balboa then deposed Fernández de Enciso on the ground that his authority was illegitimate, and a municipal council, the first in the Americas, was elected. In 1511 the settlers refused to receive Diego de Nicuesa, the governor of Veragua, and put him to sea in an unseaworthy boat that was never seen again. Balboa became governor, collecting gold from native ornaments and by violence.

On 1 September 1513 he set out across the isthmus with 190 Spaniards, native guides and dogs, fighting some caciques and allying with others. After crossing the mountains he reached the coast, walked knee-deep into the sea with a sword in one hand and a standard of the Virgin Mary in the other, and claimed the new sea and all adjoining lands for the Spanish sovereigns. He named it the Mar del Sur and the bay San Miguel, as they arrived on 29 September. He named the Pearl Islands.

The king named Pedro Arias de Ávila, known as Pedrarias Dávila, governor of Castilla de Oro, and he arrived in 1514 with 1,500 men and 17 ships. More than 500 of them died soon after reaching Darién. Balboa accepted his replacement, and the two were reconciled when Balboa was betrothed by proxy to Pedrarias's daughter María de Peñalosa. In 1518 Balboa had ships built at Acla using native labour and African slaves. He was executed by the Spanish authorities around January 1519. Panama's currency, the balboa, is named after him, and parks, avenues and an order of merit in Panama bear his name.
vasili-iv-of-russia: Born Prince Vasili Ivanovich Shuisky, he was a son of Ivan Andreyevich Shuisky and descended from the Yurievichi sovereign princes of Nizhny Novgorod, allegedly a 20th-generation male-line descendant of the 9th-century Varangian prince Rurik. He was one of the leading boyars under Feodor I and Boris Godunov, and with his brother Dmitry he usually acted in the court intrigues of the Time of Troubles. On Boris's secret orders he went to Uglich to inquire into the death in May 1591 of Tsarevich Dmitry Ivanovich, youngest son of Ivan the Terrible, and reported that it was suicide.

After Boris died and his son Feodor II acceded in 1605, Shuisky went back on his own report and recognised the pretender False Dmitri I as the real Dmitry. Shuisky then turned on the pretender, whose death in May 1606 he brought about by declaring that the real Dmitry had been killed. His adherents proclaimed him tsar on 19 May 1606. He reigned until 19 July 1610, never generally recognised.

The popularity of his cousin Prince Mikhail Skopin-Shuisky, who commanded an army aided by Swedish forces under Jacob de la Gardie, kept him on his unstable throne for a time. In 1610 the Seven Boyars, among them his former adherents Ivan Mikhailovich Vorotynsky and Fedor Ivanovich Mstislavsky, deposed him.

He was forcibly made a monk and taken with his two brothers to Warsaw by the Polish hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski. He died a prisoner in the castle of Gostynin, near Warsaw, in 1612. The Romanovs, elected rulers in 1613, recognised him posthumously as a legal tsar and during negotiations with the Polish authorities repeatedly demanded to rebury his body in Russia. After the Treaty of Polyanovka in 1635 his remains were returned to Moscow and laid in the Archangel Cathedral. He was the only member of the House of Shuisky to become tsar and the last Rurikid of the Yurievichi branch to rule as tsar.
vasily-grossman: He was born Iosif Solomonovich Grossman and did not receive a traditional Jewish education. His father, Semyon Osipovich Grossman, was a chemical engineer with social-democratic convictions who joined the Mensheviks; his mother, Yekaterina Savelievna, taught French. A Russian nanny turned the boy's name Yossya into Vasya, which the family accepted. He lived in Geneva with his mother from 1910 to 1912, moved to Kiev in 1914, and later studied chemical engineering at Moscow State University, where his diligence earned him the nickname Vasya-khimik. He then took a job in Stalino in the Donets Basin.

Grossman began writing short stories as a student. One of the first, In the Town of Berdichev, drew encouragement from Maxim Gorky and Mikhail Bulgakov, and the film Commissar (1967), suppressed by the KGB and released only in 1988, is based on it. In the mid-1930s he left his job to write full-time, and in 1937 he was accepted into the Union of Writers. His novel Stepan Kol'chugin was nominated for a Stalin prize, but Stalin himself removed it from the list for alleged Menshevik sympathies.

In 1937, during the Great Purge, his wife Olga's former husband Boris Guber was arrested, and Olga was arrested for failing to denounce him. Grossman registered as guardian of her two sons and wrote to Nikolay Yezhov, head of the NKVD, arguing that she should not answer for a man she had left long before. Olga was released. In 1941 his mother was trapped in Berdychiv and murdered with 20,000 to 30,000 other Jews. He volunteered for the front and spent more than 1,000 days there. In The Hell of Treblinka he gave 3 million as the number killed, far above the 750,000 to 880,000 now widely accepted, because of an error in his count of trains.

After the war the censors ordered changes to the Black Book, which Grossman had helped compile for the Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee, and in 1948 its Soviet edition was scrapped. The suppression shook his loyalty to the Soviet state. He died of kidney cancer on 14 September 1964 and was buried at the Troyekurovskoye Cemetery near Moscow.

Life and Fate was first published in Russian in Switzerland in 1980: Andrei Sakharov photographed draft pages kept by Semyon Lipkin, and Vladimir Voinovich smuggled the films abroad. It appeared in the Soviet Union in 1988 under glasnost and in English in 1985. Robert Chandler's revised translation of 2006 was widely praised, and some critics have compared Grossman's novels to those of Leo Tolstoy.
vasily-i-of-moscow: Vasily Dmitriyevich was born on 30 December 1371, the eldest son of Dmitry Donskoy and Grand Princess Eudoxia, daughter of Grand Prince Dmitry Konstantinovich of Nizhny Novgorod. As a young man he travelled in 1383 to the Tatar khan Tokhtamysh to obtain the khan's yarlik for his father's title of grand prince of Vladimir. He overcame the challenge of the prince of Tver, who also sought it, but was then kept at Tokhtamysh's court as a hostage until 1386, when he took advantage of the khan's conflict with Timur and escaped to Moscow.

Vasily became Grand Prince of Vladimir and Moscow in 1389. With Tokhtamysh's permission he took over Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal, which the khan gave him in exchange for help Moscow had given against a rival. He also took Murom, and in 1397–1398 Kaluga, Vologda, Veliki Ustyug and the lands of the Komi peoples were annexed. In 1392 he allied with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and married Sophia, the only daughter of Vytautas the Great. The alliance proved fragile, and the two waged war against each other in 1406–1408.

Timur raided the Volga region in 1395 but did not reach Moscow. The raid damaged the Golden Horde, which was in anarchy for the next twelve years; no tribute was paid to the khan Olug Moxammat in that time, and large sums were collected in the Moscow treasury for military purposes. In 1408 Edigu burnt Nizhny Novgorod, Gorodets, Rostov and many other towns but did not take Moscow, though he burnt it. In 1412 Vasily found it necessary to make the long-deferred visit of submission to the Horde.

In domestic affairs feudal landownership kept growing, and the judicial powers of landowners were partly transferred to Vasily's deputies and heads of volosts. Chronicles say that in 1404 the monk Lazar the Serb built a mechanical clock on a tower of the Grand Prince's Terem Palace at Vasily's request, the first in Moscow. Vasily married his daughter Anna to Emperor John VIII Palaeologus of Byzantium. Of his nine known children, only Vasily II reached mature adulthood.
vasily-ii-of-moscow: Vasily II Vasilyevich was born on 10 March 1415, the youngest son of Vasily I of Moscow and Sophia of Lithuania, the only daughter of Vytautas the Great. He was the only son to survive his father, since his elder brother Ivan died in 1417. At his father's death he was proclaimed grand prince at the age of ten, with his mother as regent. His uncle Yuri of Zvenigorod, prince of Galich-Mersky, and Yuri's sons Vasily Kosoy and Dmitry Shemyaka took the chance to press their own claims, which rested on the testament of Dmitry Donskoy, Yuri's father. Vytautas supported his grandson.

After Vytautas died in 1430, Yuri went to the Golden Horde and returned with a license to take the throne, but the khan did not support him further. In 1433 Yuri attacked Moscow and captured Vasily, who had been betrayed by the boyar Ivan Vsevolzhsky. Yuri pardoned him and sent him to Kolomna, where Vasily gathered malcontents; Yuri left Moscow. After Yuri died in 1434, Vasily Kosoy took the Kremlin until Dmitry Shemyaka allied with Vasily II and drove his brother out in 1435; Vasily Kosoy was captured and blinded.

In 1439 Vasily II fled Moscow when Ulugh Muhammad of Kazan besieged it. Six years later he led an army against Ulugh Muhammad, was defeated and captured, and was released after about five months for an enormous ransom. Dmitry Shemyaka took control of Moscow and in 1446 had Vasily blinded and exiled to Uglich, which gave him the nickname the Blind. Vasily soon gathered supporters and regained the throne. In the 1450s he captured Galich-Mersky and poisoned Dmitry, ending the struggle.

The victory settled the principle of succession from father to son against collateral succession, a major cause of medieval feuds, and paved the way for centralisation. Vasily eliminated almost all the small appanages in the Moscow principality, and his campaigns of 1441 to 1460 increased Moscow's hold over Suzdal, the Vyatka lands, Novgorod and Pskov. In 1448 a council of Russian bishops elected Jonah as metropolitan, tantamount to independence from the patriarch of Constantinople. Vasily took the title sovereign of all Russia, and made his son Ivan III co-ruler from the late 1450s. He died on 27 March 1462, and Ivan III succeeded him.
vasily-iii-of-moscow: Vasily was born on 25 March 1479, the second son of Ivan III and his second wife Sophia Paleologue. Ivan's grandson Dmitry Ivanovich became heir presumptive in 1490 and co-ruler in 1498. In 1499 Vasily was forgiven for a conspiracy against Dmitry and received the title of grand prince of Novgorod and Pskov. In April 1502 Ivan III had Dmitry and his mother Elena of Moldavia arrested and, three days later, named Vasily his successor. Vasily married Solomonia Saburova on 4 September 1505, after a bride-show of some 1,500 noble girls, a custom described by the diplomat Sigismund von Herberstein.

Vasily believed that nothing should limit the power of the grand prince, and he had the active support of the church against the boyar opposition. Those who criticised his policies were exiled or executed, among them the diplomat Ivan Bersen-Beklemishev in 1525. He continued his father's gathering of the Russian lands. In 1510 he had the leaders of the Pskov republic arrested, and the veche bell was removed and sent to Moscow; 300 of the city's most noble families were resettled on Moscow lands. In 1521 he took over Ryazan after imprisoning its prince, Ivan V Ivanovich, and he annexed the Starodub principality in 1523.

In the Lithuanian–Muscovite War he besieged Smolensk three times, with artillery and engineers supplied by the rebel Lithuanian prince Michael Glinski. The city surrendered on 31 July 1514, and a treaty of 1522 left it with Moscow. In 1521 the Crimean khan Mehmed I Giray reached the walls of Moscow and forced him to accept a treaty making him a vassal. Later campaigns brought Russian influence on the Volga, and in 1523 he founded Vasilsursk. Stone churches and fortifications were built, including the Cathedral of the Archangel in the Kremlin.

After more than twenty years of marriage with no heir, Vasily divorced Solomonia, falsely accusing her of witchcraft, and in 1526 married Elena Glinskaya. She bore a son, the future Ivan IV, and later a second, Yuri. Vasily died on 3 December 1533, after an abscess on his hip that two German doctors could not cure. He took the monastic name Varlaam before he died. He did not officially take the title of tsar, but in a treaty of 1514 with Emperor Maximilian I he was called kaiser, which Peter the Great later cited.
vassal: A vassal, or liege subject, stands in a relation of mutual obligation to a superior lord or monarch, the suzerain. The rights and duties of the vassal are called vassalage, and those of the suzerain suzerainty. A vassal is semi-independent and may rule his own country as he wishes as long as he meets his obligations. These often include paying tribute or providing military support, with knights. In return the vassal received privileges such as commerce, military protection and land held as a tenant, called a fief. Fealty, by contrast, is the sworn, unconditional loyalty owed to a monarch.

In developed European vassalage, lord and vassal took part in a commendation ceremony of two parts, homage and fealty, using Christian sacraments to show its sacred importance. According to Eginhard, the commendation made to Pippin the Younger in 757 by Tassilo III, Duke of Bavaria, involved the relics of several saints assembled at Compiegne. Such refinements were not present from the outset, in times of crisis, war and hunger, when the weakest needed the protection of the knights who owned the weapons and knew how to fight.

In the time of Charlemagne, who ruled from 768 to 814, vassalage slowly became connected with grants of land, then the main form of wealth. In Merovingian times monarchs rewarded only their most trusted vassals with lands, and even in 10th-century France most vassals still had no fixed estates. Vassals later divided into an upper group of great territorial magnates, strong enough to pass their benefice to their heirs, and a lower group of landless knights attached to a count or duke. As coordinated cavalry replaced disorganised infantry, armies became costlier, and a vassal needed land and its peasants, wood and water to equip the cavalry he owed his lord.
vastergotland: Västergötland is one of the 25 traditional provinces of Sweden, in the south-west of the country. Its north-western border is marked by Lake Vänern, Sweden's largest lake, and its north-eastern border by Lake Vättern, the second largest. The southern and eastern part is hilly, part of the southern Swedish highlands, while the northern and western portions belong to the Central Swedish lowland, the Västgöta plains, which contain hills of Silurian sedimentary rock such as Kinnekulle, Halleberg, Hunneberg and Billingen. The largest river is the Göta älv, which drains Vänern to the Kattegat, and along it several important towns have stood for centuries.

There are many ancient remains in the province, among them dolmens of the Funnelbeaker culture near Falköping and Finnestorp, near Larv, an Iron Age site of weapon sacrifices. Its people, the Geats, appear in the writings of the Greek Ptolemaios as Goutai and in Jordanes in the 6th century as Gautigoths.

Västergötland was the heartland of Götaland, once an independent petty kingdom with a long line of Geatish kings, known mainly from foreign sources and legends. When it became part of the Swedish kingdom is much debated: some date it as early as the 6th century, from the Swedish-Geatish wars in Beowulf, others as late as the 12th century.

The province received early influence from the British Isles and is generally considered the bridgehead of Christianity's advance into Sweden. Around 1000 King Olof Skötkonung is held to have been baptised at Husaby, near Lake Vänern, and because the new faith met heavy opposition elsewhere in his kingdom he had to restrict Christian activity to Västergötland.

When the provincial law, the Västgötalagen, was written in the 13th century, the province had 517 churches. The seat of the diocese was apparently first Husaby, but from 1150 it was Skara. In the civil wars that followed the election of King Stenkil in the 11th century, Swedish and Geatish dynasties vied for control, and Västergötland was several times independent under kings such as Inge I and Magnus the Strong.

Lying along the borders of Denmark and Norway, the province was often involved in armed disputes. Battles included Älgarås in 1205, Lena in 1208, Hova in 1275 and Falköping in 1389, and later the Sweden-Danish wars. In 1658 Sweden annexed the Scanian lands and Bohuslän, and the last combat on Västergötland soil came in the Scanian War of the 1670s.

Gothenburg, on the Kattegat, is its largest city. The province serves no administrative function, and since 1998 nearly all of it lies in Västra Götaland County. Skara Cathedral is the oldest cathedral in the original parts of Sweden, and Läckö Castle on Lake Vänern is regarded as one of the country's finest Baroque castles.
vasto: According to legend the town was founded by the Greek hero Diomedes, and its earliest archaeological relics date to 1300 BCE. Histonium, one of the key towns of the Frentani, did not obtain the rank of colonia under Julius Caesar but kept the title of municipium. Under the Roman Empire it was flourishing and opulent, as shown by the ruins of a theatre, baths, other public buildings, mosaics and statues. An inscription records that a thirteen-year-old boy, Lucius Valerius Pudens, won the prize for Latin poetry at a contest in Rome. The town was ravaged by the Goths, Lombards, Franks and Arabs, but probably never ceased to exist on its present site.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it fell to the Lombards and joined the Duchy of Benevento. About 774 the Franks conquered it, and in 1053 the Normans under Robert Guiscard captured it. About 1076, after raids, it was renamed Guastaymonis, the Waste of Aimone. From the 13th century it belonged to the Kingdom of Naples. In the 15th century the condottiero Giacomo Caldora, its lord, transformed its urban structure, and his family built the city walls still seen today and the Castello Caldoresco.

In 1566 Ottoman naval forces under Piyale Pasha destroyed much of the city by fire, including the Castello Caldoresco and the Palazzo d'Avalos. Under Spanish rule Vasto became a fief of the Marquis d'Avalos, and it reached its height under Cesare Michelangelo, marquis from 1697 to 1729. A short-lived Republic of Vasto in 1799 was quickly overthrown by loyalists. The poet and scholar Gabriele Rossetti was born there on 28 February 1783; exiled in 1821, he settled in London and fathered Dante Gabriel and Christina Rossetti. Fascist Italy renamed the town Istonio in 1938, and it became Vasto again in 1944.

Vasto is a comune on the Adriatic coast of the Province of Chieti, in southern Abruzzo. Its old town has buildings and churches from the 12th to the 18th centuries, among them the Cathedral of San Giuseppe, the Castello Caldoresco and the Palazzo d'Avalos, which houses the Civic Museums. The church of Santa Maria Maggiore, mentioned in a document as early as 1195, was restructured in 1735. Below the hill lies the beach resort of Marina di Vasto, and the coast to the north has typical wooden fishing machines called trabocchi.
vatican-city: The territory of Vatican City covers 44 hectares and forms part of the Vatican Hill and the adjacent former Vatican Fields, on the west bank of the Tiber. Until 1929 the area belonged to the Roman rione of Borgo. It is enclosed largely by walls: those of Leo IV (847–855), later expanded by fortifications built under Paul III (1534–1549), Pius IV (1559–1565) and Urban VIII (1623–1644).

St Peter's Square is set apart from Italian territory only by a white line along its limit. Some properties of the Holy See elsewhere in Rome and Italy, notably the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo and the major basilicas, have extraterritorial status similar to that of foreign embassies.

In the Roman Republic the name Vatican applied to the Ager Vaticanus, a marshy area on the west bank of the Tiber. Its closeness to the Etruscan city of Veii, an old enemy of Rome, and the floods of the Tiber led the Romans to regard it as dismal and ominous. Agrippina the Elder drained the area and laid out gardens there in the early 1st century CE, and in 40 CE her son, the emperor Caligula, built a circus for charioteers, later completed by Nero.

The Vatican obelisk in St Peter's Square is the last visible remnant of that circus. Caligula brought it from Heliopolis in Roman Egypt. The circus became a site of martyrdom for many Christians after the Great Fire of Rome in 64, and tradition states that Saint Peter was crucified upside-down there. In 1586 Pope Sixtus V moved the obelisk to its present position, using a method devised by the architect Domenico Fontana. The name Vatican City was first used in the Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929.

Vatican City is an absolute elective monarchy in which the pope holds legislative, executive and judicial power. Legislative authority is exercised in his name by the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, a body of cardinals appointed for five-year periods. The state is distinct from the Holy See, which has existed as a juridical entity since Roman Imperial times and was not interrupted when it lacked territory between 1870 and 1929.

Citizenship rests on appointment to work in the service of the Holy See, not on birth, and usually ends when the appointment does. In 2024 the population was 882 residents, and a further 372 citizens lived elsewhere. Legislation uses only Italian. The state earns income from stamps, coins, museum admissions and publications, and uses the euro. UNESCO listed Vatican City as a World Heritage Site in 1984, the only site that consists of an entire state.
vatican-library: Scholars have traditionally divided the library's history into five periods: Pre-Lateran, Lateran, Avignon, Pre-Vatican and Vatican. At the Lateran Palace it grew to one of the most notable collections of illuminated manuscripts in Europe, until the palace was burnt and the collection plundered by Philip IV of France in 1303. The Avignon popes added greatly to it, but between about 1370 and 1447 it was scattered, with parts in Rome, Avignon and elsewhere. Pope Nicholas V planned a public library to make Rome a place of humanist scholarship. He combined some 350 Greek, Latin and Hebrew codices from his predecessors with his own acquisitions. By 1455 it held 1,200 books, 400 of them in Greek.

Nicholas died in 1455, and Pope Sixtus IV established what is now known as the Vatican Library. Around 1481 it was the largest collection of books in the Western world. Around 1587 Pope Sixtus V commissioned the architect Domenico Fontana to build the new building that is still used today. In 1623 Maximilian I, Duke of Bavaria, gave the Palatine Library of Heidelberg, about 3,500 manuscripts that he had just taken as loot in the Thirty Years' War. The manuscripts of the Dukes of Urbino arrived in 1657, and Queen Christina of Sweden's library was bought in 1689.

During the Counter-Reformation access was limited after the Index of banned books was introduced, particularly for Protestant scholars; Pope Leo XIII formally reopened the library to scholars in 1883. In 1809 Napoleon Bonaparte had the contents seized and taken to Paris, and they were returned in 1817. Under Pope Pius XI the library was reorganised between the two world wars, and Father Franz Ehrle set up its first modern catalogue between 1927 and 1939.

The library was founded primarily as a manuscript library, and holds 75,000 codices, 1.1 million printed books including some 8,500 incunabula, and 330,000 coins and medals. Its oldest documents date from the first century. Although it has always included Bibles, canon law and theology, it specialised from the beginning in secular books, and its collection of Greek and Latin classics stood at the centre of the revival of classical culture during the Renaissance. It is open to anyone who can document their qualifications and research needs.
vatican-museums: The collection traces its origin to a single marble sculpture. Laocoön and His Sons was discovered on 14 January 1506 in a vineyard near the basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome. Pope Julius II sent Giuliano da Sangallo and Michelangelo, who were working at the Vatican, to examine it, and on their recommendation he bought it from the vineyard's owner at once. The statue shows the Trojan priest Laocoön and his two sons, Antiphantes and Thymbraeus, attacked by giant serpents. Julius put it on public display at the Vatican exactly one month after its discovery.

Later popes added separate museums. Clement XIV founded the Museo Pio-Clementino in 1771, in Innocent VIII's Belvedere Palace, and his successor Pius VI enlarged and completed it. Pius VII founded the Museo Chiaramonti in the early 19th century, and its New Wing, built by Raffaele Stern, houses the Augustus of Prima Porta and the Doryphoros. Gregory XVI founded the Museo Gregoriano Etrusco in 1837, and Pius IX founded the Lateran Museum by decree in 1854. Pius XI ordered a dedicated building for the paintings, designed by Luca Beltrami and inaugurated on 27 October 1932. The Collection of Modern Religious Art was added in 1973, the year Paul VI founded the Vatican Historical Museum.

The museums hold roughly 70,000 works, of which about 20,000 are on display, in 24 galleries, with the Sistine Chapel the last room on the visitor route. The picture gallery, the Pinacoteca Vaticana, includes Giotto's Stefaneschi Triptych, Leonardo da Vinci's Saint Jerome in the Wilderness, Raphael's Transfiguration and Caravaggio's Entombment of Christ. The Raphael Rooms contain his School of Athens, painted in 1509–1511. The Gallery of Maps, commissioned by Gregory XIII, shows topographical maps of the whole of Italy painted on the walls by the friar Ignazio Danti of Perugia. The Egyptian museum holds papyruses, sarcophagi and mummies, and the Etruscan museum vases, bronzes and terracotta.
vatican-radio: Vatican Radio began broadcasting on 12 February 1931, with the callsign HVJ on two shortwave frequencies at 10 kilowatts, with a message from Pope Pius XI, Omni creaturae. Guglielmo Marconi and Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli, the future Pope Pius XII, were present. Its first director was the physicist Giuseppe Gianfranceschi. From the start it was maintained by the Jesuit Order, and in 1936 the International Telecommunication Union recognised it as a special case, authorising broadcasts without geographical limits.

In 1933 a microwave link joined the Vatican Palace and the papal summer residence at Castel Gandolfo, and in 1937 a 25 kW Telefunken transmitter and two directional antennas were added. After a December 1939 report by Cardinal August Hlond on the oppression of the Church in Poland, Pius XII decided to use the radio to inform listeners of the Church's condition there. During World War II its news broadcasts were banned in Germany, as all foreign broadcasts were, and it operated in four languages. Jacques Adler, who examined transcripts of wartime broadcasts, argues that they exposed Nazi persecution of the Church and opposed collaboration with Nazism.

By 1948 the service had expanded to 18 languages. It was one of the 23 founding broadcasters of the European Broadcasting Union in 1950. A new broadcasting centre opened in 1957 on a 400-hectare site at Santa Maria di Galeria, north of Rome, which Italy had granted extraterritorial status in 1952. The station also made experimental television broadcasts in the 1930s.

The station's interval signal, Christus Vincit, became a well-known sound on shortwave radio. In the 21st century it moved to digital transmission, podcasts and online channels. On 27 June 2015 Pope Francis established a Secretariat for Communications in the Roman Curia, which absorbed Vatican Radio on 1 January 2017, ending 85 years of independent operation. On 24 March 2017 it made its last English-language shortwave transmission to Asia, after 59 years of service.
vaud: People lived beside the Vaud lakes in prehistoric times, and later the Celtic Helvetii inhabited the area. Caesar's troops defeated them in 58 BCE, and the Romans founded towns including Vevey and Lausanne, as well as Aventicum. Alemannic tribes invaded repeatedly between the 2nd and 4th centuries, the Burgundians occupied the territory in the 5th century and the Merovingian Franks replaced them. In 888 the area became part of the Carolingian Empire. The Zähringens defeated the Burgundians in 1032 and were succeeded in 1218 by the counts of Savoy, under whom the area gained political unity as the Barony of Vaud.

As Savoy's power declined early in the 15th century, Bernese troops occupied the land, and by 1536 Bern had annexed it. The Reformation began with co-workers of John Calvin such as Pierre Viret, but was decisively implemented only when Bern put its full force behind it. Bernese rule was unpopular: in 1723 Major Abraham Davel led a revolt over the denial of political rights to the French-speaking Vaudois, and he was beheaded.

Inspired by the French Revolution, the Vaudois drove out the Bernese governor in 1798 and declared the Lemanic Republic. French troops moved in, and Vaud became the canton of Léman in the Helvetic Republic. Unrest over the abolition of feudal rights and taxes led to the revolt of the Bourla-papey in 1802. In 1803 Vaud joined the re-installed Swiss Confederation. In November 1847 it opposed the Sonderbund, the Catholic separatist movement, in the Sonderbund War.

Vaud is one of the 26 cantons of Switzerland, with Lausanne as its capital and largest city, followed by Yverdon-les-Bains and Montreux. It is made up of ten districts and covers 3,212 square kilometres, reaching from Lake Neuchâtel to Lake Geneva and including the Jura Mountains, the Swiss Plateau and the Alps. French is its only official language, and its present constitution dates from 14 April 2003, replacing that of 1885. The Vallée de Joux is a centre of Swiss mechanical watchmaking.
vedanta: The word Vedanta means the end of the Vedas and originally referred to the Upanishads, the knowledge section of the Vedas. The Upanishads can be seen as the end of the Vedas in several senses: they were the last literary products of the Vedic period, they represent the high point of Vedic philosophy, and they were taught last, in the ascetic stage of life. Later the term came to cover the traditions that interpret three sources, the Prasthanatrayi: the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and the Bhagavad Gita. Vedanta is also called Uttara Mimamsa and counts as one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy.

All the Vedanta traditions investigate Brahman and Atman, treat scripture as the main reliable source of knowledge, and accept rebirth and the desirability of release from it, called moksha. They reject Buddhism and Jainism. They discuss three metaphysical categories: Brahman, the ultimate reality; Atman, the individual self; and the changing physical world.

The schools differ on how these relate. Advaita holds that Brahman is the sole unchanging reality, identical to the individual Atman. Vishishtadvaita, propounded by Ramanuja, holds that souls and Brahman, as Vishnu, remain different, though souls can attain a perfected spiritual body in Vaikuntha. Dvaita, taught by Madhvacharya, treats soul and Brahman as two entirely different entities. Bhedabheda traditions say the self is both different and not different from Brahman, and Vallabhacharya's Shuddhadvaita holds that the entire universe is subtly Brahman in the form of Krishna.

Little is known of Vedanta before the Brahma Sutras, whose composition is dated variously; Nakamura and Nicholson place their present form at about 400 to 450 CE. Their author Badarayana quotes six earlier Vedantic teachers whose works have not survived. Until the 11th century Vedanta was a peripheral school of thought. Gaudapada's Karika is the earliest surviving complete text on Advaita Vedanta, and Shankara is widely considered its apostle. Between the 11th and 16th centuries Vaishnava teachers such as Ramanuja, Vedanta Desika, Madhva and Vallabha challenged Shankara's doctrines.

Vedanta later became the most prominent school of Hinduism. Sri Vaishnavism rests on Ramanuja's philosophy, the Madhva tradition of coastal Karnataka on Dvaita, and many devotional traditions of north and east India on Bhedabheda. Swaminarayan founded a Vedantic tradition in 1801, and Neo-Vedanta arose in the 19th century.
vedas: The word veda means knowledge, from the Sanskrit root vid-, to know. The Vedas were composed in Vedic Sanskrit during the Vedic period, which spans the mid 2nd to mid 1st millennium BCE. The bulk of the Rigveda Samhita was composed in the Punjab in the north-west of the subcontinent, most likely between c. 1500 and 1200 BCE, though a wider range of c. 1700 to 1100 BCE has also been given. The other three Samhitas date from the time of the Kuru kingdom, c. 1200 to 900 BCE, and the commentarial and related texts, with the redaction of the Samhitas, from c. 1000 to 500 BCE.

Hindus regard the Vedas as apauruṣeya, not of a man, and as revelations heard by ancient sages after intense meditation; they are śruti, what is heard, as against smṛti, what is remembered. The Vedic hymns themselves say that sages created them skilfully, as a carpenter builds a chariot.

There are four Vedas: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda. The first three were the original division, the triple science of reciting hymns, performing sacrifices and chanting songs. Each Veda has four subdivisions: the Samhitas, which are mantras and benedictions; the Brahmanas, commentaries on rituals and sacrifices; the Aranyakas, on rituals and symbolic sacrifice; and the Upanishads, on meditation, philosophy and spiritual knowledge.

The Rigveda Samhita is the oldest surviving Indic text, with 1,028 hymns and 10,600 verses in ten books. The Samaveda has 1,549 stanzas, almost all from the Rigveda except 75 mantras. The Yajurveda is a compilation of prose offering formulas said by a priest during ritual actions. The Atharvaveda has about 760 hymns, about 160 shared with the Rigveda, and was not counted as a Veda in the Vedic era but was accepted as one in the late 1st millennium BCE.

The Vedas were transmitted orally for centuries, from teacher to student or father to son, by elaborate mnemonic techniques. Only this tradition, embodied in a living teacher, is held to give the correct pronunciation and hidden meanings. The mantras are recited for their sound rather than their meaning. The texts were kept in separate schools, or śākhās; the Rigveda that survives belongs to a single well-preserved school, that of Śākalya, from Videha in what is now north Bihar.

The Vedangas, six auxiliary fields from phonetics to astronomy, arose because the language of the Vedas had become archaic. The Vedas and these fields were part of the curriculum at ancient universities such as Taxila, Nalanda and Vikramashila. Schools of Indian philosophy that accept the Vedas' authority are called orthodox, while Buddhism, Jainism and other śramaṇa traditions that did not are called heterodox.
vedic-sanskrit: The separation of Proto-Indo-Iranian into Proto-Iranian and Proto-Indo-Aryan is estimated on linguistic grounds to have occurred around or before 1800 BCE. Asko Parpola and J. P. Mallory place the division of Indo-Aryan from Iranian in the Bronze Age Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex. In Parpola's model, early Indo-Aryans were present in the Late Harappan horizon from about 1900 BCE, and speakers of Proto-Rigvedic entered Punjab from about 1700 BCE. The date of the oldest hymns of the Rigveda is vague, generally estimated at roughly 1500 BCE.

Five chronological strata are distinguished within Vedic: the language of the Rigveda, the mantra language, the prose of the Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇa prose and the Sūtras. The first three are commonly grouped as the Saṃhitās of the four Vedas, the oldest texts in Sanskrit and the canonical foundation of the Vedic religion and of later Hinduism. Many words in the Rigveda have cognates in Avestan that do not appear in later Indian texts, and the text must have been essentially complete by around the 12th century BCE.

Vedic was preserved orally, predating the local arrival of writing by several centuries. It was far less uniform than the Classical Sanskrit described by Pāṇini, and the two differ to an extent comparable to Homeric and Classical Greek. Vedic had a tonal accent system inherited from Proto-Indo-European, and pluti, protracted vowels of three morae, which occur 3 times in the Rigveda and 15 times in the Atharvaveda.

The formalisation of the late form of Vedic into Classical Sanskrit is credited to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, together with Patanjali's Mahabhasya and Katyayana's commentary. The language of the early Upanishads approaches Classical Sanskrit. Early inscriptions of Indian rulers are in Prakrit; Sanskrit is first noticed in the inscriptions of North India from about the second half of the 1st century BCE, and it gradually displaced Prakrit in Indian epigraphy. The extensive Vedic literature that survives has been a major source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Indo-Iranian history.
veere: Veere stands on the Veerse Meer lagoon on the island of Walcheren in the province of Zeeland. The name means ferry. In 1281 Wolfert I van Borselen established a ferry and ferry house there, which he called the camper-veer, or Ferry of Campu, and until the 17th century it was known in England as Camphire. In the same year he built the castle Sandenburg on one of the dikes he had made. On 12 November 1282 Floris V, Count of Holland, issued a charter giving Wolfert sovereignty over the land and castle, and he took the title Lord Van der Veer. Veere received city rights in 1355.

The Admiralty of Veere was set up by the Ordinance on the Admiralty of 8 January 1488, in an attempt to create a central naval administration in the Burgundian Netherlands, and in 1561 the Habsburg naval forces were moved to Veere. The town was the staple port for Scotland from 1541 to 1799, and in Scotland it was known as Campvere. Until the Anglo-Dutch wars it was an important trading port.

The Flemish architects Antonis Keldermans and Evert Spoorwater designed the Grote Kerk, the fortifications, the Cisterne and the town hall. The painter Jan Gossaert van Mabuse worked at Sandenburgh castle, residence of the noble Van Borsele and Van Bourgondië families, and the poet Adrianus Valerius lived in the town from 1591. In the 17th and 18th centuries Veere was a prosperous trading city.

German infantry crossed onto Walcheren on 17 May 1940, and the Dutch garrison at Veere was ordered to surrender that evening. Scottish troops of the British 52nd (Lowland) Infantry Division liberated the town on 7 November 1944 in Operation Infatuate, and it was virtually undamaged in the fighting.

The damming of the Veerse Gat inlet in 1961 moved the fishing fleet to Colijnsplaat. Tourism is the main business. The municipality reached its present area in 1997 after seventeen historical municipalities had merged over nearly two centuries, and it has about 22,000 inhabitants; the town itself has about 1,500.
veliko-tarnovo: The old part of Veliko Tarnovo is built on three hills, Tsarevets, Trapezitsa and Sveta Gora, rising amid the meanders of the Yantra River. On Tsarevets stood the palaces of the Bulgarian emperors, the Patriarchate and the Patriarchal Cathedral, surrounded by thick walls. Trapezitsa is known for its many churches and as the former main residence of the nobility. The town has always held a strategic position on main roads connecting the western Balkans with the Black Sea and Eastern Europe with the Middle East. Its names Tarnovgrad and Tarnovo most probably come from the Old Bulgarian word for thorny, and the word veliko, meaning great, was added in 1965 in honour of its status as an old capital.

Veliko Tarnovo is one of the oldest settlements in Bulgaria, with a history of more than five millennia; the first traces of human presence, from the 3rd millennium BCE, were found on Trapezitsa. It was a stronghold of the First Bulgarian Empire, with an important military garrison. The Uprising of Asen and Peter began on 26 October 1185, the feast day of St. Demetrius of Thessaloniki, and ended with the restoration of Bulgaria as the Second Bulgarian Empire, ruled by the Asen dynasty, with Tarnovo as capital.

From the 12th to the 14th century Tarnovgrad was the strongest Bulgarian fortification and its most prosperous city, and the political, economic, cultural and religious centre of the empire. It covered about 70 hectares across the hills. The Bulgarian cleric Gregory Tsamblak described it in the 14th century as a very large, handsome city surrounded by walls, with 12,000 to 15,000 inhabitants. The Ottoman Empire captured it on 17 July 1393 after a three-month siege in which the Bulgarian Patriarch Evtimiy led the defence, and three years later conquered the entire Bulgarian Empire.

On 7 July 1877 the Russian general Joseph Vladimirovich Gourko liberated the city, ending 480 years of Ottoman rule. In 1878 the Treaty of Berlin created a Principality of Bulgaria between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, with its seat at Veliko Tarnovo. In the early 1950s, under Communist rule, the city underwent intensive urbanisation, expanding to the west.

Veliko Tarnovo is the administrative centre of Veliko Tarnovo Province in north central Bulgaria, often called the City of the Tsars. It had 68,783 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It is the seat of Veliko Tarnovo University, and its monuments include the Monument to the Asen Dynasty, built in 1985.
veliky-novgorod: Veliky Novgorod lies on the Volkhov River, 6 kilometres downstream of its outflow from Lake Ilmen, on the road between Moscow and Saint Petersburg. Its name means Great Newtown, and the epithet distinguished it from other Russian towns called Novgorod. The earliest settlement is thought to have stood at the source of the Volkhov, where Ryurikovo Gorodishche was founded in the 9th century. By 930 the elite residences outside that fort had merged at the present site, and reliably dated archaeological layers there begin in the 930s. The name was first given to the detinets, or kremlin, and later extended to the whole city.

The Nikon Chronicle, a late source, mentions the city under 859, in connection with the death of the elder Gostomysl, while the Primary Chronicle in the Laurentian Codex has it under 862. The city's charter accepts 859, a date proposed by the historian Mikhail Tikhomirov in 1959. Lying on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks, Novgorod became the second most important city of Kievan Rus', and the eldest son of the ruling Kievan prince was customarily sent to rule it.

In 1136 the Novgorodians dismissed their prince, Vsevolod Mstislavich, and this year traditionally begins the Novgorod Republic, which lasted until 1478. It was a city-state dominated by a small group of wealthy merchant and noble families, unusual in Russia, where princes typically held supreme authority. It controlled much of the Russian North, from the Gulf of Finland to the Ural Mountains, traded with the Hanseatic League, whose kontor there was the Peterhof, and was one of Europe's largest cities at its peak in the 14th century.

Ivan III abolished some elective offices after the incorporation into the Russian state. In 1570 the oprichniki of Ivan IV sacked the city, and the historian Ruslan Skrynnikov counted 2,170-2,180 recorded deaths, a figure he did not consider final. After the capital moved to Saint Petersburg in 1712 Novgorod lost its commercial importance.

German forces occupied the city from 19 August 1941 until the Red Army liberated it on 20 January 1944, by which time only 40 of 2,346 residential buildings were undamaged and 65 architectural monuments had been destroyed or badly damaged. Its chief monuments and those of its surroundings were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1992. It is the administrative centre of Novgorod Oblast, and the population was 224,286 in the 2021 census. Archaeological research has been systematic since 1932.
veliky-ustyug: Veliky Ustyug stands near the confluence of the Sukhona, flowing from the west, and the Yug, flowing from the south. Below the junction the rivers form the Northern Dvina. The name Ustyug means the mouth of the Yug, and by the late 15th century it had become Veliky, or Great, Ustyug. The first recorded settlement was the monastic settlement at Gleden, where the Troitsko-Gledensky Monastery now stands. The historic centre lies on the high left bank of the Sukhona, in an area that was once a posad, a craftsmen's quarter outside the fortress.

A chronicle first mentions the town in 1207, and the Mikhaylo-Arkhangelsky Monastery was founded in 1212. It belonged to the Vladimir-Suzdal Principality, while neighbouring lands such as Totma were colonised by Novgorod, so it formed the only obstacle to Novgorod's trade with the north along the Sukhona and the Northern Dvina. Clashes between Novgorod and Ustyug became regular, especially in the 14th century. The Grand Duchy of Moscow annexed the town in 1328. The Mongol invasion did not directly affect it, and in the second half of the 13th century it grew rapidly with refugees from central Russia.

In 1450 Dmitry Shemyaka took the town during his war with his cousin Vasily II of Moscow, drowned in the Sukhona the citizens who refused to accept him as prince, and held it for two years. Polish troops besieged the town in 1613, during the Time of Troubles, but never took it. At the junction of important trade routes it became a significant commercial and industrial centre in the 16th and 17th centuries. It was also known for silver filigree, birch bark fretwork and niello, for its own Ustyug icon painting and for tiles.

Veliky Ustyug lost its key role as a river port when trade between China and western Europe was diverted to the Baltic after the founding of Saint Petersburg in 1703. It has preserved almost all of its architectural monuments, with churches and cathedrals of the 17th and early 18th centuries, among them the Assumption Cathedral, built between 1619 and 1659. The museum director Nikolay Bekryashev, from 1924 to 1938, persuaded the authorities to hand old churches to the museum rather than demolish them. Many of the town's heritage buildings stand on the left bank of the Sukhona. In Vologda Oblast, it is mostly known for tourism.
velleius-paterculus: Few details of Velleius' life are known with certainty, and even his first name is uncertain: Priscian calls him Marcus, but the first printed edition of 1520 calls him Publius and elsewhere Gaius. Most of what is known comes from his own brief account in his history. He was born into a noble Campanian family, though the place of his birth is unknown, and was a great-great-great-grandson of Minatus Magius of Aeculanum in Samnium, who received the Roman franchise for his actions during the Social War. His uncle Capito sat in the Roman Senate.

As a young man Velleius served as a military tribune in Rome's eastern provinces. In 2 CE he was with the army of Gaius Caesar and witnessed his meeting with Phraates V of Parthia on the banks of the Euphrates. Two years later he was a cavalry prefect in the command of Tiberius in Germania, and he remained a senior member of Tiberius' staff until 12 CE. He was elected quaestor, filling the office in 7 CE. Augustus designated him and his brother Magius Celer for the praetorship before he died, and the two were formally elected under Tiberius and served in 15 CE.
He was among the friends of Sejanus, whom he praises in his writing. There is no evidence that he outlived his friend's downfall by long, and it seems likely that he shared his fate.

His Roman history, in two books, was apparently conceived as a universal history. The first book runs from the aftermath of the Trojan War to the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE and is missing several portions, including its beginning. The second, intact, runs from the age of the Gracchi to 30 CE. It is the only connected narrative of much of that period, since Livy's books on the late Republic are lost, and it is especially detailed from the death of Caesar to that of Augustus. It consists largely of highlights and character portraits, and its showy rhetoric is typical of Silver Age Latin; judgements of its quality vary considerably.

The work seems to have been little known in antiquity. A badly damaged manuscript found at Murbach Abbey in Alsace in 1515, since lost, formed the basis of the first printed edition, published by Beatus Rhenanus in 1520.
velletri: Velletri lies about 40 km to the south-east of the centre of Rome, in the Alban Hills of Lazio. Its northern territory stands on the southern foothills of the Colli Albani range, formed about 150,000 years ago after the collapse of the volcano Laziale, while its southern boundary reaches the Pontine Marshes, whose reclamation began under Pope Pius VI and was completed under Benito Mussolini. The square of the Trivium in the old town stands at 332 metres above sea level, and the climate is mild and very rainy.

The Latin term for a swamp was Velia, and the name Velitrae is thought to come from the same root. Tradition says the town came into conflict with Rome under Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of Rome, who besieged it after the Volsci plundered Roman territory; its elders surrendered and a treaty of peace and friendship followed. Its massive Volscian walls were razed in 338 BCE as a punishment after the final Roman conquest, and they were not rebuilt until the Middle Ages.

Velletri declined after it was sacked by Alaric the Goth in 410 CE. It was a bishopric, and after the Byzantine reconquest of Italy it became an imperial city. In 592 Pope Gregory I joined the Diocese of Tres Tabernae to that of Velletri. In the Middle Ages it was one of the few free cities of Lazio, and its motto, Est mihi libertas papalis et imperialis, claims liberty from both pope and empire. The bell tower of Santa Maria in Trivio was raised in 1353 in thanks for deliverance from the plague of 1348.

During the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748), Bourbon troops defeated the Austrian Habsburgs at the Battle of Velletri. After the French Revolution the town rebelled and was proclaimed a republic, which lasted until 1814. In 1849 Giuseppe Garibaldi defeated a Bourbon Neapolitan force there, but the Roman Republic was overwhelmed soon after. Fierce fighting took place around the town in 1944, after the Anglo-American landing at Anzio.

Velletri is an Italian comune in the Metropolitan City of Rome. Its Cathedral of St Clement was built in the 4th century over a pagan temple and rebuilt in 1659-1662. The Oreste Nardini Civic Archaeological Museum holds the Sarcophagus of the Labors of Hercules, of the 2nd century. The bronze sheets of Velletri, found in 1784 within the Church of St Francis, are kept at the National Archaeological Museum of Naples. The surrounding country is known for its wine, and the town was a regular stop between Rome and Naples on the Grand Tour.
vellore: Vellore lies on the banks of the Palar River in the Palar basin, surrounded by the Javadi Hills, an extension of the Eastern Ghats, about 135 kilometres west of Chennai. It is the administrative headquarters of Vellore district. According to one legend the name comes from the many babul trees, called velan trees locally, that surrounded the region; another story says the god Murugan, with the epithet Velan, came to the place in anger. Because of its importance and its position relative to Madras it has also been called the Second Madras.

The recorded history of Vellore goes back to the ninth century, as a Chola inscription in the Annamalaiyar Temple at Tiruvannamalai shows. Many dynasties dominated it, among them the Pallava dynasty, the Medieval Cholas, the Rashtrakuta dynasty, the Sambuvaraya chieftains, Vijayanagar, the Nawabs of the Carnatic and the British. The fort and the Jalakandeswarar Temple inside it date from the Vijayanagara period; because records are lacking, the fort's exact date of building is not known. The Aravidus lost Vellore to the Bijapur Sultan before the Marathas captured it in 1676 after a siege of four and a half months. It passed to the British in 1760, and the fort withstood Hyder Ali's siege from 1780 to 1782.

After Tipu Sultan was killed at Sringapatam, the British exiled his surviving children and their households to Vellore Fort, where they took part in the mutiny of 1806. In 1805 the new commander of the Madras Army, General Sir John Cradock, had approved regulations on uniform and appearance: Hindus were forbidden religious marks on the forehead on duty, Muslims had to shave their beards, and a new headdress with a leather cockade offended upper-caste sepoys, for whom leather was a taboo. Many sepoys came to believe their officers meant to convert them to Christianity.

Vellore Fort, a Monument of National Importance managed by the Archaeological Survey of India, has a broad moat, granite ramparts broken by round towers, and within it a church, a mosque and a Hindu temple. Tipu Sultan's family and the last king of Sri Lanka, Vikrama Rajasinha, were held there as prisoners. The Christian Medical College and Hospital, founded in 1900 by the American medical missionary Ida S. Scudder, has grown into an institution of international standing. Vellore is also a centre of the leather industry.
velvet-revolution: The Communist Party seized power in Czechoslovakia on 25 February 1948, and no official opposition parties operated afterwards. Dissidents, notably those of Charter 77, published home-made periodicals, and the secret police persecuted them. People were blacklisted for signing Charter 77, supporting Alexander Dubček during the Prague Spring, promoting religion or having family in the West, and as all schools, media and businesses belonged to the state the rules were easy to enforce. By the late 1980s discontent with living standards had grown, and the changes in neighbouring countries, among them the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989, encouraged protest.

On 17 November 1989, International Students' Day, about 15,000 people joined a demonstration in Prague, which marked the fiftieth anniversary of the killing of the student Jan Opletal by the Nazi authorities. Riot police stopped the marchers on Národní Street and attacked them. A false report that a student, Martin Šmíd, had been killed spread the next day and persuaded hesitant citizens to join the protests. Students and theatres went on strike, and on 19 November Václav Havel and other dissidents founded the Civic Forum in Prague, with Public Against Violence formed the same day in Bratislava.

The number of protesters in Prague grew from 200,000 to an estimated 500,000 by 20 November. The entire Presidium of the Communist Party, including General Secretary Miloš Jakeš, resigned on 24 November, and on 27 November a two-hour general strike took place across the country, supported by a reported 75 per cent of the population. The Federal Assembly then removed the constitutional provision for the party's leading role. On 10 December President Gustáv Husák swore in the first government in 41 years not dominated by the Communist Party, and resigned.

Havel was elected president of Czechoslovakia on 29 December 1989, and Alexander Dubček became speaker of the federal parliament the day before. Havel negotiated the removal of about 73,500 Soviet troops, who left within months. Free elections in June 1990 were the first democratic ones since 1946, and Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 31 December 1992. The name Velvet Revolution was coined by Rita Klímová, the dissidents' English translator. Slovaks have called the events the Gentle Revolution. Some theorists, among them Jaroslav Krejčí, argue it was not a true revolution because it involved no illegitimate violence.
veneto: Veneto covers 18,398.9 square kilometres in the north-east of Italy. It is bordered by Friuli-Venezia Giulia to the east, Emilia-Romagna to the south, Lombardy to the west and Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol to the north, and in its northernmost corner it touches Austria. The climate is continental on the plains and milder along the Adriatic coast, around Lake Garda and in the hills. Rainfall is scarce near the river Po, about 750 millimetres a year, and much greater in the Prealps. The region is divided into seven provinces: Belluno, Padua, Rovigo, Treviso, Venice, Verona and Vicenza.

Between the 2nd and 1st millennium BCE the region was inhabited by the Euganei. Ancient historians derived the Veneti from Paphlagonia in Anatolia, led by Prince Antenor, a comrade of Aeneas, at the time of the fall of Troy, which may have been an attempt to link Venetic origins with the legend of Roman origins in Troy. Other historians link them with the Celts. In the 3rd century BCE the Veneti sided with Rome, and during the Second Punic War they sent soldiers against Hannibal, some of whom were killed at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE. The region remained part of the Roman Empire until the 5th century CE.

By the middle of the 8th century the Franks controlled the mainland, which became part of the Carolingian Empire. When invaders threatened the wealth of the mainland, part of the population took refuge on islands in the lagoon, where Venice arose. It became an independent maritime republic ruled by an elected doge, and it ruled the region until 1797. Napoleon's armies conquered Veneto in 1805–1806, and after the Congress of Vienna of 1814–1815 it formed the eastern half of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia within the Austrian Empire. The region joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866 after the Third Italian War of Independence and a plebiscite.

Veneto is one of the 20 regions of Italy, with 4,857,460 inhabitants. Venice is the capital and Verona the largest city. Most inhabitants speak Venetian as well as Italian. The regional Statute, first promulgated on 22 May 1971, speaks of the Venetian people, though the region does not have the special statute of its neighbours Friuli-Venezia Giulia and Trentino-Alto Adige. Under Austrian rule the agricultural economy suffered, and nearly 3 million Venetians left between 1861 and 1961, many for Brazil and Argentina. Millions of people of Venetian descent now live abroad, especially in southern Brazil, where places such as Nova Veneza and Nova Treviso recall their origin.
venice: Venice is built on an archipelago of more than a hundred islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, an enclosed bay of about 550 square kilometres between the mouths of the Po and the Piave. The islands are separated by canals and linked by several hundred bridges, and the historic centre is divided into six districts, or sestieri. Those who sought refuge on the islands of Torcello, Iesolo and Malamocco learned to drive closely spaced piles of alder trunks into the mud until they reached compressed clay, and laid plates of Istrian limestone on top. Subsidence contributes to the seasonal acqua alta, when the lowest surfaces are covered at high tide.

No surviving record deals directly with the founding of Venice. Tradition and the evidence have led several historians to agree that the first inhabitants were refugees from nearby Roman cities such as Padua, Aquileia, Treviso, Altinum and Concordia, and from the countryside, fleeing Germanic and Hun invasions. The traditional founding is the dedication of the church of San Giacomo on the islet of Rialto, said to have taken place at noon on 25 March 421. The city was the capital of the Republic of Venice from 810 to 1797, when Napoleon ended its sovereignty, and in 1866 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

Early prosperity probably owed much to the trade in slaves captured in central Europe and sold to North Africa and the Levant. The city later controlled a vast sea empire and was considered the first real international financial centre, reaching its fullest prominence in the 14th century. The Venetian Arsenal, the base of its naval power, is considered by several historians to be the first factory in history. Its population was 60,000 in 1000, 80,000 in 1200, between 110,000 and 180,000 in 1300, and approached 200,000 by 1600.

The municipality had 254,850 residents in 2021, of whom 50,434 lived in the historic island city. Within the historic centre transport remains entirely on water or on foot, and the gondola survives mainly for tourists and ceremonies. The lagoon and the city were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Marco Polo and Giacomo Casanova were Venetian writers, and the composers Tomaso Albinoni and Antonio Vivaldi were born there.
venlo: Roman and Celtic coins have been found at Venlo. It was speculated to be the settlement called Sablones on the Roman road between Maastricht and Xanten, though what little evidence there is goes against this. Documents of the 9th century mention it as a trade post, and it became one of the more important ones in the Meuse-Rhine area. It received city rights in 1343 and joined the Hanseatic League in 1375.

Because of its strategic importance Venlo was besieged several times, the most significant siege being that of 1702, carried out by Menno van Coehoorn. By the Treaty of 1713 it was incorporated into the Generaliteitslanden of the United Provinces, and after the Napoleonic Wars it became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. At the start of the Belgian Revolution of 1830 Venlo, like most of Limburg, sided with the Belgian rebels and was then Belgium's northernmost fortress. In 1839 King William I signed the Treaty of London recognising Belgian independence, and Belgium gave up parts of Limburg, including Venlo, to the Dutch. From 1839 to 1866 the city was completely surrounded by the territory of the German Confederation without belonging to it.

On 9 November 1939 two British Intelligence Service agents were kidnapped by the Sicherheitsdienst in the Venlo Incident, which the Nazis used to link Britain to Georg Elser's failed attempt on Hitler's life the day before and to justify the invasion of the Netherlands on 10 May 1940. Between 13 October and 19 November 1944 bombing raids on the road and railway bridges over the Meuse killed about 300 people and destroyed much of the historic city, though the Stadhuis and the Römer house survived. Allied forces liberated Venlo from the east.

Venlo lies in the province of Limburg, close to the German border. In 2001 the municipalities of Belfeld and Tegelen were merged into it, and Arcen en Velden followed in 2010. It is linked to Germany by two motorways and by a junction railway station. Greenport Venlo is one of five designated Greenports in the Netherlands and its second largest concentration of horticulture. Higher education is provided by Fontys University of Applied Sciences, the HAS University of Applied Sciences and Maastricht University Campus Venlo, and the city hosted Floriade 2012, a horticultural exhibition.
ventspils: Ventspils lies in the historical region of Courland in north-western Latvia, where the Venta river reaches the Baltic Sea. Its name means castle on the Venta, after the castle that the Livonian Order built beside the river. Historically it was known as Windau in German. In the Russian Empire it was called Vindava or Vindau, and the form Ventspils has been used since the Second World War. Its harbour does not freeze, which has made it an important port.

The town grew up around the Livonian Order's castle and was chartered in 1314. It became an important merchant city of the Hanseatic League. Under the Duchy of Courland it flourished as a shipbuilding centre, where 44 warships and 79 trading ships were built, and the duke's fleet that set out to colonise Gambia and Tobago sailed from Ventspils. Metal, amber and wood-working shops also contributed to its growth. The Polish-Swedish War and the Great Northern War destroyed the town, and a plague in 1711 killed most of the remaining inhabitants. After the Third Partition of Poland-Lithuania in 1795 it came under the Russian Empire.

Shipbuilding and trade did not matter again until about 1850. The port was modernised in the 1890s and linked to Moscow by rail, and it became one of the most profitable ports of Imperial Russia, with a yearly profit of 130 million rubles by 1913. The population grew from 7,000 in 1897 to 29,000 in 1913, then fell by almost half during the German occupation of 1915 to 1919.

The Red Army set up a base in 1939, and the city was under Soviet occupation from 1940 and German occupation from 1941 to 1944. In Soviet times an oil pipeline was built to the port, which became the USSR's leading port for crude oil export.

Ventspils is the sixth-largest city of Latvia, and it remains an ice-free port from which oil and other minerals from Russia are loaded. It has an international airport and a high technology park. The Old Town keeps 17th-century storehouses near the Market Square, and a house built in 1646 at the crossing of Tirgus and Skolas Streets is among the oldest of its type in Latvia. The city hosts the Sea Festival every July, and since 2006 an International Writers' and Translators' House has stood in the former City Hall of 1850. Ventspils University College is among its institutions of higher education.
venus-de-milo: The Venus de Milo is made of Parian marble and stands over 2 metres high, larger than life size. The flesh is polished smooth, while chisel marks remain on other surfaces. The drapery is more elaborately carved on the right than on the left, and the back is less finely finished, which suggests the figure was meant to be seen only from the front. The body is realistic, but the head is more idealised, with small eyes and mouth and slightly open lips. Stylistically it combines classical elements, such as the strong brow and nose, with Hellenistic ones, such as the shape of the torso and the deeply carved drapery.

A Greek farmer found the statue on 8 April 1820 on the island of Milos, then part of the Ottoman Empire. Olivier Voutier, a French sailor interested in archaeology, witnessed the discovery. A hand holding an apple, an arm fragment and two herms were found alongside it. The Comte de Marcellus bought the statue as it was being loaded onto a ship for another buyer. Louis XVIII had it installed in the Louvre, unrestored.

The goddess has usually been identified as Aphrodite holding the apple of discord, though other proposals include Amphitrite, a Muse, Nemesis and Sappho. In the 19th century the consensus placed her in the fourth century BCE. In 1893 Adolf Furtwängler argued that she was late Hellenistic, a dating widely accepted since. The original position of the arms is still uncertain; Wilhelm Fröhner suggested in 1876 that the right hand held the slipping drapery and the left an apple.

Within a few years of the discovery, according to Kenneth Clark, the statue took the central place once held by the Venus de' Medici. In the 19th century it was distributed in plaster casts, photographs and bronze copies. In 1964 it was exhibited in Tokyo and Kyoto, the only time it has left France since the Louvre acquired it. More than 70 poems have been written about it, and René Magritte and Salvador Dalí took it up in the 20th century. Martin Robertson thinks its reputation owes more to propaganda than to artistic merit.
venustiano-carranza: José Venustiano Carranza de la Garza was born on 29 December 1859 in Cuatro Ciénegas, Coahuila, into a prosperous cattle-ranching family of Basque descent. His father, Jesús Carranza Neira, fought on the Liberal side in the Reform War and against the French intervention, and Benito Juárez rewarded him with land that became the basis of the family's fortune. Venustiano entered politics in 1887 as municipal president of Cuatro Ciénegas and served as a senator for his state under Porfirio Díaz.

He grew disillusioned with Díaz's authoritarian rule and backed Francisco Madero in 1910. Madero made him minister of war on 3 May 1911, though he had contributed little to the rebellion, and as governor of Coahuila from 1911 he pursued reforms of the judiciary, tax laws and workplace safety, and invested in education.

When Madero was murdered in February 1913, Carranza issued the Plan of Guadalupe against Huerta and, as Primer Jefe, forged a northern coalition, the Constitutionalists. After Huerta fell in July 1914 the coalition split: the Convention of Aguascalientes rejected Carranza, and Pancho Villa allied with Emiliano Zapata. Álvaro Obregón's loyalty, the oil-rich Gulf Coast and the ports of Veracruz and Tampico gave Carranza the means to win, and Obregón defeated Villa at Celaya in April 1915.

The convention at Querétaro met in December 1916, with 85 delegates close to Carranza and 132 radicals who insisted on land reform. Article 27 of the new constitution declared that private property had been created by the Nation, which could regulate it. The constitution was proclaimed on 5 February 1917, and Carranza became constitutional president in May. He achieved little change in office, and kept Mexico neutral in the First World War. He ordered Zapata's assassination in 1919.

In 1920 Carranza endorsed the obscure diplomat Ignacio Bonillas as his successor. Obregón, Plutarco Elías Calles and Adolfo de la Huerta issued the Plan of Agua Prieta, and Carranza fled the capital and was assassinated, on 21 May 1920. The Sonoran leaders left him out of the official memory of the Revolution, but his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in 1942.
veracruz: Veracruz, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave, is one of the 31 states that with Mexico City make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It lies in eastern Mexico and borders Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo, Puebla, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco. It is a crescent-shaped strip between the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Gulf of Mexico, about 650 kilometres from north to south with an average width of about 100 kilometres, and covers 78,815 square kilometres. Its coastline runs for 690 kilometres, and the land rises from coastal plains to the Pico de Orizaba, at 5,636 metres Mexico's highest peak.
The state is divided into 212 municipalities. The suffix of its name honours Ignacio de la Llave y Segura Zevallos, governor in 1855 to 1857 and again in 1861 to 1863.

Before the Spanish arrival the region was populated mainly by four Indigenous groups: the Huastecs and Otomis in the north, the Totonacs in the centre-north and the Olmecs in the south. Archaeological remains survive at Cempoala, El Tajín, San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán and Tres Zapotes, among other sites.

Hernán Cortés and his expedition founded Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz on 18 May 1519, the first Spanish town in what is now Mexico. By doing so Cortés overthrew the authority of the governor of Cuba, Diego Velázquez, and claimed authority directly from the Spanish Crown. During the Mexican War of Independence much of the state backed the insurgents, who held most of it for the rest of the war, although the commercial class of the port did not support them.

In 1905 more than 5,000 workers of the El Valle Nacional company struck, and strikes at factories in Rio Blanco and Orizaba led to violence in January 1907. No major battles of the Mexican Revolution were fought in the state, but in 1917 Venustiano Carranza temporarily moved the federal government there.

The capital is Xalapa-Enríquez, usually called Xalapa. Other large cities include Veracruz, Boca del Río, Coatzacoalcos, Córdoba, Minatitlán, Orizaba and Poza Rica. Its economy has long rested on agriculture and petroleum, and the Laguna Verde Nuclear Power Plant lies in Alto Lucero.
veracruz-city: Veracruz, also known as Heroica Veracruz, is the municipal seat of the municipality of Veracruz on the Gulf of Mexico, 90 km (56 mi) south-east of the state capital Xalapa. The area is flat, at an average altitude of ten metres above sea level, with a tropical savanna climate and a wet season that lasts from June to October. Part of the city extends into the neighbouring municipality of Boca del Río.

The name comes from the Latin Vera Crux, True Cross. Hernán Cortés founded the settlement of Villa Rica on Good Friday, 22 April 1519, and dedicated it to the True Cross. It was the first Spanish settlement on the mainland of the Americas to receive a coat of arms. The Spanish captain Juan de Grijalva, with Bernal Díaz del Castillo, had first arrived in 1518 at the island later known as San Juan de Ulúa.

In the colonial period the port was the most important in New Spain, and its merchants formed a mercantile class larger and at times wealthier than that of Mexico City. Turkeys, corn, beans, avocados and cotton were exported to Spain, and fava beans, wheat, rice, cattle, pigs, fabric and wine came in return. From the mid sixteenth century gold and silver were the chief exports, carried on the treasure ships of the Spanish treasure fleet. This wealth attracted pirates, mostly from Britain and Holland, such as Francis Drake and John Hawkins, and Fort San Juan de Ulúa was built against them.

After independence in 1821 the city twice earned the title of Heroic City, for its defence against a French attack during the Pastry War and against American forces in 1847. In the Mexican–American War the siege continued until 27 March 1847, when General Juan Morales began to negotiate with General Winfield Scott, and on the 29th the city and San Juan de Ulúa were occupied. About five thousand prisoners and four hundred pieces of artillery were taken. American forces attacked and occupied the port again between April and November 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, in a dispute with President Victoriano Huerta, and the city gained its fourth title.

Veracruz is the most populous city of its state, with 537,952 inhabitants at the 2020 census.
