The Port of Veracruz is the oldest and largest in Mexico, and its economy has recovered since the later twentieth century. Its culture blends indigenous, Spanish and Afro-Caribbean elements, seen in its son jarocho music and its cuisine, including red snapper Veracruz-style. The Veracruz Carnaval has been held every year since 1866, in the reign of Maximilian I.
veraguas-province: Veraguas lies in the centre-west of Panama and covers 10,587.6 square kilometres. It is the only Panamanian province with coastlines on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, but most of its people live on the Pacific side, and the Caribbean coast is mostly uninhabited. It is said that the name comes from the indigenous word Veracua or Viragua, though other theories exist. The province is divided into 12 districts, subdivided into 104 corregimientos, and had 259,791 inhabitants in 2023.

Veraguas was originally inhabited by the Veraguas culture. Christopher Columbus explored it on his fourth voyage and tried to establish the first colony on the new Spanish mainland, but failed because of resistance from Indigenous peoples. Diego de Nicuesa also tried to found a colony and failed, which led him to create a colony from which to fight the Indigenous population, which he named Nombre de Dios.

The capital, Santiago de Veraguas, was founded about 1636. A province called Veraguas that contained Santiago, but whose boundaries changed over time, existed in Gran Colombia, in the Republic of New Granada and at times during the Panama State era.

The people of Veraguas are mainly of Spanish and Indigenous origin and are known as campesinos. The province has forests, mountains, coasts and islands, with more than 200 varieties of orchids and more than 400 species of birds. Its national parks include Coiba National Park, which has the largest coral reef on the Pacific coast of America, Cerro Hoya National Park on the Azuero Peninsula and Santa Fe National Park, a forest in the north. The church of San Francisco de la Montaña, in Baroque style, dates from 1727 and was declared a National Historical Monument on 27 January 1937.
vercingetorix: Vercingetorix belonged to the Arverni, a people of what is now Auvergne. Their king Bituitus was decisively defeated by Rome in 121 BCE, and the Arverni later abandoned kingship for an oligarchy like that of their rivals the Aedui. Vercingetorix was probably born at their chief town Gergovia. His birth year is inferred from Caesar calling him a young man in 52 BCE, and scholars place it in the 80s or 70s BCE. His father Celtillus was murdered by fellow aristocrats, around 70 to 60 BCE, for trying to restore kingship. His name probably means supreme king of warriors and may be a title rather than a birth name. Nearly all that is known comes from Caesar, who describes him through a Roman lens.

In early 52 BCE, after the Carnutes massacred Romans at Cenabum, Vercingetorix tried to raise the Arverni, but his uncle Gobannitio and other aristocrats exiled him. He rallied countryside followers, retook Gergovia and was proclaimed king. About ten peoples joined, and he imposed harsh discipline. When Caesar took Vellaunodunum, Cenabum and Noviodunum, Vercingetorix adopted scorched-earth tactics, but the Romans stormed Avaricum, where only about 800 of the reported inhabitants escaped. At Gergovia he drove Caesar back, one of only three recorded Roman defeats of the Gallic Wars. The Aedui then joined him, and an assembly at Bibracte made him sole commander.

A cavalry defeat sent him into the Mandubian town of Alesia, which Caesar surrounded with siege works. The Gauls expelled women, children and the old, whom Caesar refused to admit; they starved between the lines. A relief army failed in three assaults, and Vercingetorix accepted responsibility, saying the war had been fought for collective freedom, and offered himself to spare his people.

Plutarch has him ride out in fine armour, circle Caesar and sit at his feet; Cassius Dio, thought more plausible, says he hoped for pardon because of past friendship with Caesar. He was held six years in the Tullianum, shown in Caesar's triumph in 46 BCE and executed there, possibly by strangulation. Zecchini suggests Caesar could not appear pro-Gallic while Roman opinion was hostile to the Gauls.

Largely forgotten in the Middle Ages, Vercingetorix was rediscovered in the 16th century. In 19th-century France, especially after 1871, he became a symbol of national identity and of the noble loser. Napoleon III financed excavations at Alesia and commissioned a bronze statue there by Aimé Millet. Painters such as Lionel Royer in 1899 fixed the image of the Gaul throwing down his weapons.
verdun: Verdun stands on both banks of the Meuse in the north of the Meuse department, in Grand Est. It lies 225 km from Paris and 184 km from Strasbourg, and is the largest city of the department, although the prefecture is Bar-le-Duc, 47 km to the south. The Gauls founded it, and its Latin name, Verodunum, is a latinisation of a Gaulish place name meaning strong fort. In 486 it refused to yield to the Franks after their victory in the Franco-Roman War and was besieged by King Clovis I.

Verdun became a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire in 1374, and with Toul and Metz it formed the Three Bishoprics. A large bastioned citadel was built from 1624 to 1636 on the site of the Abbey of Saint Vanne. In 1670 Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban visited and drew up a scheme to fortify the whole city; much of it was carried out in the following decades, and some elements were finished only after the Napoleonic Wars, when the citadel held British prisoners of war.

In the War of the First Coalition the fortress was captured on 20 August 1792 by the Prussians, who opened the path to Paris but abandoned Verdun after the Battle of Valmy. In the Franco-Prussian War it was the last French fortress to surrender, in 1870. A new system followed, a ring of 22 polygonal forts up to 8 kilometres from the city and an inner ring of 6.

The battle of 1916 began on 21 February with a bombardment by over 1,000 German guns commanded by Erich von Falkenhayn. The Germans took Douaumont on 25 February; Philippe Pétain then organised the defence and kept open the supply road from Bar-le-Duc, which became known as the Voie Sacrée. Fort Vaux fell on 7 June, and the Anglo-French offensive on the Somme from 1 July drew the Germans away. Estimates put the dead at 143,000 Germans and 162,440 French. French counter-attacks under Robert Nivelle regained the forts by the end of the year.

The Châtel Gate is the only surviving part of the medieval walls, and the 17th-century Citadel is still in military hands, though its tunnels can be visited. Verdun Cathedral was consecrated in 1147, and the Episcopal Palace was built in the 18th century by Robert de Cotte. On the battlefield stand French and German cemeteries; the largest is the French National Cemetery and Douaumont Ossuary, which holds roughly 130,000 unidentified remains. In 1916 King George V awarded the city the Military Cross.
verica: Verica's coinage presents him as a son of Commius and king of the Atrebates, a tribe that was probably Belgic. His predecessors are likely to have influenced a wide area covering Berkshire, Surrey, western Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The distribution of his own coins shows a much smaller kingdom, limited to modern Sussex and east Hampshire, with its capital in or near the later Roman town of Noviomagus Reginorum, the modern Chichester. He succeeded his elder brother Eppillus in about 15 CE.

He may also have ruled the northern Atrebatic kingdom at Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester. Rome recognised him as rex, and he appears to have had friendly trading and diplomatic links with the empire, perhaps in an attempt to restore the kingdom to its former strength. Unlike those of nearby areas, the hillforts in the core of his kingdom show no sign of refortification, which implies that its inhabitants were well disposed to Rome.

The Catuvellauni pressed on his territory from the east. Epaticcus, brother of Cunobelinus, conquered Calleva in about 25 CE. After the death of Epaticcus about 35 CE Verica regained some territory, but Caratacus, the son of Cunobelinus, conquered the entire kingdom some time after 40 CE. By the time of his expulsion the kingdom had been reduced to a core around Chichester and the Manhood Peninsula.

Dio Cassius records that a Berikos, widely taken to be Verica, fled to the emperor Claudius because of a revolt, and Suetonius mentions British demands that Rome return certain deserters. His ties with Rome have been used to argue that the invasion landed on the south coast and not at the traditional site of Richborough in Kent. He may have been restored afterwards, but this is not attested, and a new ruler of the region, Cogidubnus, soon appeared; he may have been Verica's heir.

Most scholars take Verica to have been a man. The archaeologist Miles Russell has argued that Verica was a woman, citing the ending of the name and the horsewomen on the coinage. Roger Tomlin disputes this, since no female client ruler is known to have used the title rex, and Daphne Nash notes that some coins show Verica with an Adam's apple and in male priestly dress.
verkhovna-rada: The word Rada means council. The institution originated in the time of Kievan Rus', when it was a council of boyars and of the higher clergy. In the 17th and 18th centuries the Zaporozhian Cossacks used the term for the meetings where major decisions were made, and they elected new councils by popular vote. The Ukrainian People's Republic had a Central Rada between 17 March 1917 and 29 April 1918. The present name comes from the Soviet practice of calling national and republican parliaments Supreme Soviets, a term localised in the Ukrainian SSR as Verkhovna Rada.

The Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR was set up under the 1937 constitution, with its first elections on 26 June 1938 and its first session in Kyiv from 25 to 28 July 1938. Its first chairman was Mykhailo Burmystenko. During the Second World War its Presidium was evacuated to Saratov, and it returned to Kyiv in 1944.

The first partially free elections were held on 4 March 1990. The Communist Party remained in control, but a Democratic Bloc that included the People's Movement of Ukraine (Rukh) was formed. The new parliament issued the Declaration of State Sovereignty on 16 July 1990 and declared independence on 24 August 1991, under its chairman Leonid Kravchuk. A national referendum overwhelmingly supported the act on 1 December 1991. The Constitution of Ukraine was adopted on 28 June 1996.

The Verkhovna Rada is the sole body of legislative power. It has 450 deputies, elected by equal and direct universal suffrage by secret ballot, and it elects a chairman and two deputy chairmen from among its members. It adopts laws, amends the constitution, approves the state budget, appoints the prime minister, ratifies treaties and declares war and peace. Bills are usually considered in three readings, and the president must sign a law before it is promulgated. Electoral systems have varied: all seats were filled in single-member districts in 1990 and 1994, half in 1998 and 2002, and by party lists alone in 2006 and 2007.

The parliament meets in a neo-classical building on Mykhaila Hrushevsky Street in Kyiv, designed by Volodymyr Zabolotny after a competition in 1936. It was built from 1936 to 1938, destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt from 1945 to 1947.
versailles: The Palace of Versailles stands in the north-western part of the commune of Versailles, about 16 kilometres south-west of Paris, in the Yvelines department. The name covers both the main building and the wider estate, which includes the Grand Trianon, the Petit Trianon, the Grand Canal and the park. The palace covers about 63,154 square metres and contains roughly 2,300 rooms. The park now covers 815 hectares, compared with more than 8,000 hectares before the French Revolution.

The site is first mentioned in 1038 in an abbey charter. In the 16th century the land belonged to the Gondi family, and Louis XIII bought part of it in 1623 and the rest in 1632. In 1668 and 1669, after the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, Louis XIV decided to turn Versailles into a full royal residence. From 1668 to 1671 the architect Louis Le Vau encased Louis XIII's château on three sides in a new building known as the enveloppe, which gave an Italianate façade towards the gardens.

Louis XIV used the palace to promote himself and to centralise royal power, beginning with nighttime festivals in the gardens in 1664, 1668 and 1674. The king, the court and the government lived there permanently from 6 May 1682 until 6 October 1789, except during the Regency years of 1715 to 1723. Jules Hardouin-Mansart enlarged the palace in the 1680s, and Ange-Jacques Gabriel remodelled the Ministers' Wings in the 1770s.

Napoleon considered making Versailles his residence but abandoned the idea because of the cost, and had the Grand Trianon restored in 1810. Louis XVIII and Charles X did not live there either. In June 1919, after six months of negotiations, the Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors.

The palace is owned by the French state and has been run since 1995 as a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture. It houses the National Museum of the History of France. Restoration work began in 1892 under the first conservator, Pierre de Nolhac, and John D. Rockefeller Jr. gave funds for it between 1925 and 1928. The restoration of the Hall of Mirrors was completed in 2006.
verviers: Verviers lies roughly halfway between Liège and the German border. It is the centre of an agglomeration that includes Dison and Pepinster, the second biggest in the province of Liège. Water has played an important part in its economy, first in the development of its textile industry and later of its tourist industry. Many fountains have been built in the city, and it is called Wallonia's Water Capital. Flint and bone fragments and Roman coins found in the area attest to early settlement.

After the Romans failed to hold back Germanic tribes in the 4th century, Clovis's Salian Franks occupied the region at the end of the 5th. The Verviers area was forested and became a hunting ground for the Merovingian kings, who kept a vicus in neighbouring Theux, and monks of the nearby Abbey of Stavelot slowly made it Christian. Late in the 10th century Charles the Simple ceded the Marquisate of Franchimont to Notker of Liège, who was consolidating the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Liège took direct control of the marquisate in 1014, and Frederick Barbarossa and Pope Adrian IV confirmed this in 1155.

A textile industry in the area is first mentioned in the 15th century. The Eighty Years War in the neighbouring Netherlands helped the cloth industry to replace the older metallurgical works. The town stayed modest in size until 1651, when the expansion of its fulleries led to its recognition as one of the prince-bishopric's bonnes villes, or main cities. The annexation of Liège to France in 1795 caused a steep economic decline and unprecedented poverty.

The city's fortunes rose after the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. William Cockerill, who brought his knowledge of the machines of British industry, introduced mechanisation to the factories of Iwan Simonis. Roads were paved, gas lighting was installed, and the city doubled in size during the Industrial Revolution. Verviers lay at the eastern end of the sillon industriel, the industrial backbone of Wallonia. After the First World War it could share with Bradford the title of Wool Capital of the World. Its factories could not face international competition from the 1950s and closed one after another. The Wool and Fashion Tourist Centre now stands in a former factory, and the Grand Theatre was built at the end of the 19th century.
via-egnatia: The Via Egnatia crossed the Roman provinces of Illyricum, Macedonia and Thracia, in what is now Albania, Greece, North Macedonia and European Turkey. From Dyrrachium, today Durrës, it followed the river Genusus, now the Shkumbin, over the Candaviae mountains and on to the highlands around Lake Ohrid. It then turned south through high mountain passes to the northern coast of the Aegean at Thessalonica, and from there ran through Thrace to Byzantium.

The main literary source for its building is Strabo's Geographica, together with milestones found along the route. Bilingual inscriptions on the milestones record that Gnaeus Egnatius, proconsul of Macedonia, ordered its construction, and the road presumably took its name from him. The exact date is uncertain. It may have replaced an earlier military road from Illyria to Byzantium, described by Polybius and Cicero, which the Romans built over or improved.

The road was built to link a chain of Roman colonies stretching from the Adriatic to the Bosphorus. Its western end lay almost directly opposite the end of the Via Appia, so the colonies of the southern Balkans had a direct connection to Rome. Until a more northerly route across Illyria was opened under Augustus, it was Rome's main link with its empire in the eastern Mediterranean. It was repaired and extended several times but suffered long periods of neglect during Rome's civil wars.

It figured in several moments of Roman history. The armies of Julius Caesar and Pompey marched along it in Caesar's civil war, and Mark Antony and Octavian pursued Cassius and Brutus along it to the Battle of Philippi. The Apostle Paul used it on his second missionary journey, travelling from Philippi to Thessalonica. Surviving milestones record that the emperor Trajan carried out extensive repairs before his campaign of 113 against the Parthians.

By the 5th century CE the road had largely fallen out of use because of violent instability in the region, and a historian of that century noted that its western sections were barely passable. It revived as a key road of the Eastern Roman Empire. Procopius records repairs by the emperor Justinian I in the 6th century, though the road was said to be almost unusable in wet weather. Almost all Byzantine overland trade with western Europe used it, and armies of the Crusades travelling east by land followed it to Constantinople. A modern Greek highway, the Egnatia Odos, takes its name from the road. The Aromanians call the old road Calea Mare, the Big Road.
vibo-valentia: Vibo Valentia was originally the Greek colony of Hipponion, founded, probably in the late seventh century BCE, by settlers from Locri, a principal city of the region on the Ionian Sea. Its city wall, 7 km in circumference, enclosed the hill and ran down to the port. It had cylindrical towers at intervals, and its monumental size testifies to the wealth of the city and the wars it fought. Diodorus Siculus reports that Dionysius the Elder, tyrant of Syracuse, took the city in 388 BCE and deported its whole population. The people returned in 378 BCE with Carthaginian help, and Hipponion later came under the Bruttii, who controlled most of present Calabria.

After the town fell to Rome its name was Latinised to Hipponium, and it became a Roman colony as Vibo Valentia. It prospered in the late Republic and early Empire, and Cicero had a villa there. A diocese was established in 451 and suppressed in 1083, when it was incorporated into the Diocese of Mileto. The town was almost completely abandoned after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. In 1070 the Normans built a castle on the site of the old acropolis, and in 1235 Frederick II, Holy Roman emperor and king of Sicily, established a new city with the name of Monteleone.

The town took back its old Roman name only in 1928, having been called Monteleone di Calabria from 1861. It is the capital of the province of Vibo Valentia and a commune of 30,753 inhabitants, near the Tyrrhenian Sea, with the harbour of Vibo Marina important to its economy. About 350 metres of the Greek walls survive, including the foundations of eight towers, each with an estimated height of 10 metres. The Norman-Hohenstaufen castle, built of materials from nearby Greek temples and damaged by the earthquake of 1783, houses a state museum. The cathedral, dedicated to Santa Maria Maggiore e San Leoluca, was built in the ninth century over a Byzantine basilica.
vicente-guerrero: Vicente Guerrero was born in Tixtla, a town in the Sierra Madre del Sur about 100 kilometres inland from Acapulco. He worked in his father's mule-driven freight business, which took him across Mexico and exposed him to ideas of independence. He joined the insurgent army of José María Morelos in late 1810. Because he spoke Nahuatl, he was able to recruit support among Indigenous communities, and in a speech at Tlapa in 1815 he argued for citizenship to be extended to Indigenous people.

After Morelos was captured and executed in December 1815, Guerrero became one of the last major insurgent commanders in the field. From 1816 to 1821 he kept the war alive by guerrilla warfare in the Tierra Caliente, refusing viceregal offers of pardon even when his father carried an appeal for him to surrender.

In 1821 Guerrero held the royalist commander Agustín de Iturbide to a stalemate and appealed to him to join the cause of independence. The Plan of Iguala of 24 February 1821 proclaimed independence and a constitutional monarchy, kept the place of the Catholic Church and made all inhabitants citizens without distinction of European, African or Indian origins. Their combined forces entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821. In 1823 Guerrero joined the rising against Emperor Iturbide, and he was afterwards named one of the ruling triumvirate.

The September 1828 election, decided by the state legislatures, went to Manuel Gómez Pedraza, with Guerrero second. Antonio López de Santa Anna rose in support of Guerrero, fighting broke out in Mexico City, and Gómez Pedraza resigned and went into exile. Guerrero took office on 1 April 1829 with the conservative Anastasio Bustamante as vice president. Facing an empty treasury and a Spanish attempt at reconquest, he used extraordinary powers to abolish slavery across almost all of Mexico in September 1829, though he exempted Texas on 2 December 1829 under pressure from settlers.

Bustamante's rebellion began on 4 December 1829, and Guerrero was deposed on 17 December. He withdrew to the south and fought through 1830. In January 1831 the Italian captain Francisco Picaluga, who was paid 50,000 pesos by the government, invited him aboard his ship at Acapulco and handed him to federal troops. After a court-martial he was shot at Cuilapam on 14 February 1831, an act the liberal press called judicial murder.

His remains were returned to Mexico City in 1842. The state of Guerrero is named for him, and his reported reply to his father, La Patria es Primero, is written in gold inside the Chamber of Deputies.
vicenza: Vicenza lies at the northern base of Monte Berico, where it straddles the River Bacchiglione, about 60 kilometres west of Venice. Three of its bridges over the Bacchiglione and the Retrone are of Roman origin, and isolated arches of a Roman aqueduct stand outside the Porta Santa Croce.

The site was settled by the Italic Euganei and then by the Paleo-Veneti in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. In 157 BCE the city was a de facto Roman centre, called Vicetia or Vincentia, 'victorious', and its citizens received Roman citizenship in 49 BCE. It was known for agriculture, brickworks, a marble quarry and wool. The city recovered from raids after the Ostrogoth conquest in 489, was soon taken by the Byzantine Empire, and was later a Lombard and Frankish centre.

Magyar raiders destroyed Vicenza in 899. In 1001 Otto III handed the government to the bishop, but the commune soon separated from episcopal authority and joined the Lombard League against Frederick I Barbarossa. Frederick II sacked it in 1237. In 1311 it submitted to the Scaligeri lords of Verona. It came under Venetian rule in 1404, and in 1496 the podestà Antonio Bernardo expelled the Jews. After 1797 it passed to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and then to Austria, rose against Austria in 1848, and was annexed to Italy after the Third Italian War of Independence. It was the most damaged city in Veneto in Allied bombing in the Second World War.

Twenty-three buildings by Andrea Palladio stand in Vicenza, among them the Basilica Palladiana in the Piazza dei Signori and the Teatro Olimpico, begun in 1580, the year he died. UNESCO inscribed the city as a World Heritage Site in 1994 and extended the listing in 1996 to the Palladian villas of the Veneto. Textile, steel and jewellery industries are central to its economy.
viceroyalty-of-new-spain: After the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1521, Hernán Cortés named the territory New Spain and set the capital, Mexico City, on the site of Tenochtitlan. The Kingdom of New Spain was established on 18 August 1521 under the Crown of Castile. It was a kingdom and not a colony, subject to the monarch in Spain, who held sovereignty and property rights over it. With the political and economic importance of the conquest, the crown asserted direct control, and on 12 October 1535 it created the viceroyalty by royal decree, appointing as viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, an aristocrat loyal to the monarch rather than to Cortés. Peru followed as the second viceroyalty in 1542.

The viceroy lived in Mexico City and was appointed by the monarch, but most matters were handled by local bodies, first among them the audiencias, which were superior tribunals with administrative and legislative functions and answered to the Council of the Indies. Second-level divisions were the captaincies general: Santo Domingo (1535), the Philippines (1565), Puerto Rico (1580), Cuba (1608), Guatemala (1609) and Yucatán (1617). Spanish Florida and Spanish Louisiana were governorates. Through the Patronato real the crown oversaw the Church in everything but doctrine.

Early on, conquistadors received grants of native tribute and labour known as encomiendas, modelled on the tribute and corvée labour that the Mexica rulers had demanded. In practice the system often intensified exploitation. The discovery of silver at Zacatecas in the 1540s drew Spanish miners and crown officials, and silver mining enriched both the colony and the crown. Acapulco was the American terminus of the transpacific trade with the Philippines by the Manila galleon. Mexico City was the seat of the viceroy, the archbishop, the Inquisition and the merchants' guild.

The history of mainland New Spain spans three hundred years, from the conquest of 1519-1521 to the Mexican War of Independence of 1810-1821. In the eighteenth century the Bourbon Reforms created intendancies, increased the military presence and centralised royal authority, and the Jesuits were expelled.

At its widest extent the crown claimed all of modern Mexico and Central America except Panama, most of the United States west of the Mississippi, the Floridas, the Spanish West Indies, and the Philippines, the Mariana Islands and the Caroline Islands, though it did not control large parts of this. After Napoleon's invasion of Iberia in 1808 and the forced abdication of Charles IV, a crisis ended the government of Viceroy José de Iturrigaray. The viceroyalty was dissolved in 1821 and the Mexican Empire was established, with Agustín de Iturbide crowned emperor.
viceroyalty-of-peru: Francisco Pizarro and his conquistadors arrived in Peru in 1532, and the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire is traditionally dated from the encounter at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532. Atahualpa was taken prisoner and executed on 26 July 1533. Pizarro founded Lima on 18 January 1535 as the City of the Kings. The conquerors then fell into conflict among themselves, and to end it King Charles I of Spain signed the New Laws in Barcelona on 20 November 1542. They established the Viceroyalty, officially the Kingdom of Peru, in place of the governorships of New Castile and New Toledo, and moved the seat of the Audiencia of Panama to Lima.

After almost forty years of administrative disorder, Viceroy Francisco de Toledo established between 1569 and 1581 the political and administrative framework that governed for many years. Between 1580 and 1650 large-scale mining took hold, with the silver of Potosí refined by amalgamation using mercury from Huancavelica. Silver production peaked in 1610. In the Bourbon period the viceroyalty lost territory: New Granada was created in 1717 and re-established permanently in 1740, and the Río de la Plata in 1776. Lima lost its place as the economic centre, though Peru remained the Crown's most valuable asset in South America.

Viceroy José Fernando de Abascal made Peru the centre of the royalist counter-revolution, and all attempts at independence, such as the Cuzco Rebellion of 1814, were suppressed. The Capitulation of Ayacucho, signed on 9 December 1824, ended the royalist military effort, and the last strongholds, the Real Felipe Fortress at Callao and the Chiloé Archipelago, fell in 1826.

The rest of the viceroyalty depended administratively on Lima, whose University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, is the oldest institution of higher education on the American continent. The economy rested on silver, mined by contract and free wage labourers and by the mita, a system of unfree labour inherited from pre-Hispanic times. A census by the last quipucamayoc recorded 12 million inhabitants of Inca Peru, and under Toledo, 45 years later, the figure was 1,100,000 Indians, a loss attributed largely to smallpox and other Eurasian diseases. Inca cities were rebuilt as Spanish towns around a plaza, and the Church was prominent: in the 17th century, Lima, with 26,000 inhabitants, had nineteen churches and monasteries.
vichy: Vichy is a city in the department of Allier, on the river Allier, with about 25,000 inhabitants. Its mineral springs are rich in trace elements such as lithium and fluorine and high in sodium bicarbonate. They owe their warmth to volcanic activity in the nearby Massif Central, and about 289 springs have been charted in the town and its surroundings. The name is the French form of the Occitan Vichèi, of uncertain etymology; one proposal derives it from a Latin Vippiacus, after a landowner presumably called Vippius. The cold soup vichyssoise is named after the town.

The first known settlement was founded by Roman legionaries in 52 BCE, who found the hot springs on their way south after their defeat at Gergovia by the Gauls under Vercingetorix. They called the township Aquae Calidae, "Hot Waters". In 1344 John II of France ceded the fiefdom to Peter I, Duke of Bourbon, and by 1374 it was wholly in the House of Bourbon's hands. A Celestinian monastery was founded in 1410. By the end of the 16th century the baths drew patients from the noble and wealthy classes, and the marquise de Sévigné, a patient in 1676 and 1677, popularised them in her letters.

Napoleon III's stays between 1861 and 1866 transformed the town: dikes were built along the Allier, 13 hectares of gardens replaced the marshes, chalets and pavilions were built for his court, and a large casino opened in 1865. The Opera House and the Hall of Springs were inaugurated in 1903. Vichy welcomed 40,000 curistes in 1900 and nearly 100,000 just before the First World War, and thermal life reached its height in the 1930s.

After the defeat of 1940 the French government fled Paris and, finding Clermont-Ferrand too cramped, moved to Vichy on 1 July. The town lay in the unoccupied zone and had the second largest hotel capacity in the country. On 9 and 10 July, 670 of the 846 members of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies voted full powers to Philippe Pétain. The new regime called itself the French State but became known as Vichy France. Germany occupied the Free Zone in November 1942. The city was liberated without bloodshed on 26 August 1944.

In 2021 Vichy became part of the transnational UNESCO World Heritage Site Great Spa Towns of Europe. Vichy Pastilles are octagonal candies made from the soda in the spring waters, and the name Vichy is used for a brand of the L'Oréal company. A term of the war years must not be confused with its inhabitants: partisans of the Pétain regime are called Vichyste, while residents are Vichyssois.
victor-amadeus-ii: Victor Amadeus was born in Turin on 14 May 1666, the only child of Charles Emmanuel II and Marie Jeanne Baptiste of Nemours. His father died in June 1675, and his mother ruled as regent, known at court as Madame Royale, until he banished her from the state's affairs in 1684. She had tried to arrange his marriage to his first cousin Infanta Isabel Luísa of Portugal, which would have kept her permanently in control; he refused, and the plan came to nothing. Under pressure from Louis XIV and his mother he instead married Anne Marie d'Orléans, by proxy at Versailles on 10 April 1684 and in person on 6 May.

Under his mother's regency Savoy had been a French satellite. At Louis XIV's urging Victor Amadeus began a persecution of the Vaudois in 1685, but his alliances with England and the Dutch Republic in the Nine Years' War forced him to stop in 1688, and in 1694 he granted an Edict of Toleration. He broke with France by joining the Grand Alliance in that war, and he enlarged his army from about 8,500 to more than 24,000. In the War of the Spanish Succession he changed sides again, joining the Grand Alliance in 1703. Turin was besieged in 1706 and saved in September by the combined forces of Victor Amadeus and Prince Eugene of Savoy.

He reformed the state. In 1696 he set up a system of intendants on the French model to collect taxes and keep order, and in 1697 he began a land survey, the Perequazione, of the holdings and privileges of the Church and nobility. In 1717 he created separate secretaries for war, internal affairs and foreign affairs. He established a select militia in 1690 and overhauled it in 1714, and from 1713 began a navy. He was crowned King of Sicily at Palermo on 24 December 1713, and after objections from an alliance of four nations he exchanged it in 1720 for the poorer kingdom of Sardinia.

In 1730 Victor Amadeus married Anna Canalis di Cumiana, and in September abdicated in favour of his son Charles Emmanuel III. After a stroke in 1731 he wished to resume the throne, and his son had him arrested and held at Moncalieri. He died on 31 October 1732. He reigned for over 55 years, the longest of any Savoyard ruler, and left a cultural mark on Turin, remodelling the Royal Palace and the Palace of Venaria and building the Basilica of Superga.
victor-amadeus-iii-of-sardinia: Victor Amadeus was born on 26 June 1726 at the Royal Palace of Turin, the eldest son of King Charles Emmanuel III and his second wife, Polyxena of Hesse-Rotenburg. He was styled Duke of Savoy from birth until he succeeded to the throne. His education was entrusted to Gerdil Giacinto Sigismondo, with particular emphasis on military training. He is said to have been privately conservative, and his father felt him unsuitable to hold power.

On 31 May 1750 at Oulx he married Infanta Maria Antonia of Spain, youngest daughter of Philip V of Spain and Elisabeth Farnese. The marriage was arranged by her half-brother Ferdinand VI and served to strengthen relations between Madrid and Turin after the War of the Austrian Succession. The couple had twelve children, among them the later kings Charles Emmanuel IV, Victor Emmanuel I and Charles Felix.

Victor Amadeus succeeded on 20 February 1773 and began by working on bureaucratic and military matters. On the advice of the bourgeoisie and aristocracy he set up two new cultural state institutions. He had the port of Nice improved and dams and the road of the Côte built. In 1785 he created the Società Agraria di Torino, and he encouraged the extension of the Orto Botanico dell'Università di Torino. Although politically conservative, he carried out numerous administrative reforms until he declared war on Revolutionary France in 1792. At the outbreak of the Revolution he gave his sons-in-law, the Counts of Artois and Provence, shelter in his kingdom. On 21 May 1793 he established the Gold Medal of Military Valour.

In April 1796 the French under Napoleon Bonaparte beat the Piedmontese army at Montenotte (12 April), Millesimo (13–14 April) and Mondovì (21 April). On 26 April they proclaimed the Republic of Alba in the occupied territories, and two days later, by the Armistice of Cherasco, it was ceded back to Victor Amadeus. On 15 May he was forced to sign the Treaty of Paris, abandoning the First Coalition. He ceded the fortresses of Cuneo, Ceva, Alessandria and Tortona, allowed French armies free passage towards Italy, and gave up Nice and Savoy.

He died on 16 October 1796 at the Castle of Moncalieri after an attack of apoplexy, leaving an economically struggling kingdom, and was buried at the Basilica of Superga in Turin. In 1786 he had moved the remains of many of his ancestors and kinsmen there.
victor-emmanuel-ii: Victor Emmanuel was born in the Palazzo Carignano in Turin, the eldest son of Carlo Alberto, Prince of Carignano, who in 1831 succeeded a distant cousin as King of Sardinia. He spent some years of his youth in Florence and showed an early interest in politics, the military and sports. In 1842 he married his cousin Adelaide of Austria, and they had eight children. He fought in the front line under his father in the First Italian War of Independence, at Pastrengo, Santa Lucia, Goito and Custoza.

Charles Albert abdicated in 1849 after defeat by the Austrians at the Battle of Novara, and Victor Emmanuel obtained a favourable armistice at Vignale from the Austrian commander Radetzky. When the Chamber of Deputies refused to ratify it, he dismissed his Prime Minister, Claudio Gabriele de Launay, and appointed Massimo D'Azeglio; after new elections the peace was accepted. In 1849 he also suppressed a revolt in Genoa. In 1852 he appointed Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, who modernised the kingdom for war, and in 1855 Sardinia joined Britain and France in the Crimean War, which gave it a place at the peace conference.

At Plombières in 1858 Cavour and Napoleon III agreed that France would receive Nice and Savoy in return for help against Austria. After the campaign of 1859 Napoleon III made a separate treaty at Villafranca, giving Piedmont only Lombardy and leaving Venetia to Austria; Cavour resigned, then returned, and the Treaty of Turin of March 1860 gave France Nice and Savoy. Plebiscites joined Tuscany, Modena, Parma and Romagna to Piedmont-Sardinia. The king's forces defeated the papal army at Castelfidardo, and he was excommunicated. He met Garibaldi at Teano and received control of the south, and on 17 March 1861 he was proclaimed first King of Italy, keeping his old numeral and making Turin the capital.

In 1866 he allied with Prussia and received Veneto after the Austrian defeat in Germany. After the French withdrew in 1870 he entered Rome on 20 September, and the capital was set up there on 2 July 1871, with the Quirinal Palace as the royal residence, after a temporary move to Florence in 1864. His part in day-to-day government gradually dwindled, as ministers in practice became responsible to Parliament.

Victor Emmanuel died in Rome in 1878, after envoys of Pope Pius IX had lifted his excommunication and he had received last rites. He was buried in the Pantheon and succeeded by his son Umberto I. Italians gave him the epithet Padre della Patria, Father of the Fatherland, and he became the symbol of the Risorgimento. The Victor Emmanuel II Monument in Rome, containing the Altare della Patria, was built in his honour.
victor-emmanuel-iii: Victor Emmanuel was born in Naples on 11 November 1869, the son of Umberto I and Margherita of Savoy, who were first cousins. On 24 October 1896 he married Princess Elena of Montenegro, and on 29 July 1900 he became king at the age of 30, after his father was assassinated by an anarchist. The Statuto Albertino left the king considerable residual powers, among them the right to appoint a prime minister who lacked a majority in the Chamber of Deputies.

The first fourteen years of the reign were dominated by the prime minister Giovanni Giolitti, who pursued industrialisation and brought in universal male suffrage. When the First World War began Italy stayed neutral, then signed the secret Treaty of London in April 1915. The Chamber forced Antonio Salandra to resign, but the king declined his resignation and personally decided that Italy would enter the war. Victory brought Trento, Trieste and South Tyrol, and he was called the King of Victory.

In 1922 Benito Mussolini led the March on Rome. Prime Minister Luigi Facta drafted a decree of martial law, but the king, after some hesitation, refused to sign it, doubting that the army could contain the rising without a civil war. He then appointed Mussolini. He took no action against the regime's abuses, among them the murder of Giacomo Matteotti in 1924, though critics held that he could have dismissed Mussolini then. In 1936 he took the crown of Emperor of Ethiopia after the invasion that the League of Nations condemned, and in 1939 that of King of the Albanians; he also stayed silent when racial laws were issued.

In 1939 he held back Mussolini from entering the war, telling Count Galeazzo Ciano that Italy was in no condition to wage war, but he gave him sweeping powers in June 1940. After the Allied invasion of Sicily he dismissed Mussolini in July 1943 and appointed Pietro Badoglio. The armistice of Cassibile followed in September, and the king fled to Brindisi. After the liberation of Rome in June 1944 he transferred most of his powers to his son Umberto.

He abdicated on 9 May 1946 in favour of Umberto II, hoping to strengthen the monarchy before the referendum of 1946, which established the Republic. He went into exile in Alexandria, where he died on 28 December 1947. His decisions to take the crowns of Ethiopia and Albania and his silence over Fascist abuses are held to have proved fatal to the monarchy.
victor-horta: Victor Horta was born in Ghent on 6 January 1861, the son of a master shoemaker who considered craftsmanship a high form of art. He began studying music at the Royal Conservatory of Ghent but was expelled for misbehaviour and went to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts there. At seventeen he moved to Paris and worked for the architect Jules Debuysson.

After his father died in 1880 he returned to Belgium, settled in Brussels and studied architecture at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, where he became friends with Paul Hankar and was taken on as an assistant by his professor Alphonse Balat, architect to King Leopold II. With Balat he worked on the Royal Greenhouses of Laeken, his first use of glass and iron. He admired the theorist Eugène Viollet-le-Duc throughout his life.

Horta's breakthrough came in 1892, when he was commissioned to design a house for the scientist Émile Tassel. The Hôtel Tassel, completed in 1893, has a fairly traditional stone facade, but the interior is built around an open central stairway, with curling lines modelled on vines and flowers repeated in the ironwork, floor tiles, glass and painted walls. It is widely recognised as one of the first appearances of Art Nouveau in architecture.

Further town houses followed: the Hôtel Solvay for Armand Solvay, the Hôtel van Eetvelde with its winter garden, and his own house and studio. In 1896 to 1899 he built the Maison du Peuple for the Belgian Workers' Party, a functional steel structure with a hall seating over 2,000, demolished in 1965 despite a petition by over 700 architects.

After about 1900 his buildings became simpler, and after he returned from the United States in 1919 he abandoned organic forms for geometrical ones. His later works include the Centre for Fine Arts in Brussels, built between 1923 and 1929, and Brussels-Central railway station. He was named a baron by King Albert I in 1932. He died on 8 September 1947, still working on the station, which was completed by his colleagues led by Maxime Brunfaut and opened on 4 October 1952.

The novel element in Horta's houses was his search for maximum transparency and light on the narrow building sites of Brussels, achieved with large windows, skylights, mirrors and open floor plans. He designed furniture and details to match each house, down to the bronze doorbell of the Hôtel Solvay.

His curving vegetal forms influenced Hector Guimard in Paris, and he is also considered a precursor of modern architecture. After Art Nouveau lost favour, many of his buildings were abandoned or destroyed. In 2000 UNESCO listed four of his Brussels town houses: the Hôtel Tassel, the Hôtel Solvay, the Hôtel van Eetvelde and the Horta House, now the Horta Museum.
victor-hugo: Victor-Marie Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 in Besançon, the youngest son of Joseph Léopold Sigisbert Hugo, a general in the Napoleonic army, and Sophie Trébuchet. His father was an atheist and an ardent supporter of the Republic, while his mother was loyal to the deposed dynasty. Because his father was an officer, the family moved often from posting to posting. In 1810 his father was made Count Hugo de Cogolludo y Sigüenza by Joseph Bonaparte, then King of Spain, though the Spanish title seems not to have been legally recognised in France.

In his youth Hugo resolved to be Chateaubriand or nothing, and his life came to parallel that of the older writer in many ways. Like him, he furthered the cause of Romanticism, became involved in politics and was forced into exile. He married Adèle Foucher in October 1822.

Hugo published his first novel, Hans of Iceland, in 1823 and his second, Bug-Jargal, in 1826. His five volumes of poetry between 1829 and 1840 cemented his reputation as one of the great elegiac and lyric poets of his time. The Hunchback of Notre-Dame appeared in 1831 and Les Misérables in 1862. He was at the forefront of Romanticism with his play Cromwell and his drama Hernani. After three unsuccessful attempts he was elected to the Académie française in 1841, and he wrote the libretto of Louise Bertin's opera La Esmeralda in 1836.

Politically he moved from royalism toward republicanism. Louis Philippe I appointed him a peer of France in 1845, where he spoke against the death penalty and social injustice and for freedom of the press. Elected in 1848 to the National Assembly of the Second Republic as a conservative, he broke with the conservatives in 1849 with a speech calling for an end to misery and poverty. His campaign to abolish the death penalty was known internationally.

When Louis Napoleon seized complete power in 1851, Hugo openly declared him a traitor to France. He moved to Brussels, then to Jersey, from which he was expelled for supporting the newspaper L'Homme. He settled at Hauteville House in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, in self-imposed exile from October 1855 until 1870. He returned to Paris in 1870 and was hailed as a national hero. He lost a bid for re-election to the National Assembly in 1872 and was elected to the new Senate on 30 January 1876.

Hugo died on 22 May 1885, aged 83. He was given a state funeral in the Panthéon of Paris, attended by over two million people, the largest in French history. He produced more than 4,000 drawings, with about 3,000 surviving. His portrait was placed on French currency.
victoria-and-albert-museum: The museum traces its origins to the Government School of Design, set up by the British government in 1832 at Somerset House in London for the direct application of the arts to manufactures. The government feared that poor art education was restricting the growth and export potential of British industry. The school included a museum that held plaster casts of ancient sculptures and architectural features for teaching. By February 1854 discussions were under way to move it to Brompton, where Prince Albert was planning a group of institutions as a legacy of the Great Exhibition, nicknamed Albertopolis by the press.

Henry Cole persuaded the authorities to rename Brompton as South Kensington, and in 1857 the museum moved there as the South Kensington Museum. Queen Victoria opened it on 20 June 1857. In its first fifty years it formed part of the national system of art education, and its School of Design component became the National Art Training School, later the Royal College of Art. Aston Webb won the competition of 1891 to design the Cromwell Road front, and at the foundation stone ceremony on 17 May 1899 the new name was announced.

In the Second World War many objects were sent to quarries, a country house and tunnels near two tube stations, while the Raphael Cartoons were bricked up in the basement. After the war the Britain Can Make It exhibition of 1946 drew nearly one and a half million visitors. The fifteen British galleries were rebuilt and reopened in 2001, and the Medieval and Renaissance galleries opened in November 2009.

The collection spans 5,000 years and numbers about 2.83 million objects. It holds the largest ceramics collection in the world, with over 80,000 objects, and more than 53,000 textiles. Its sculpture collection is the most comprehensive holding of post-classical European sculpture, and the Asia collection exceeds 160,000 objects, with South Asian art the most important in the West. The Jameel Gallery of Islamic Art, opened in 2006, has the Ardabil Carpet as its centrepiece.

The museum also houses the National Art Library and, since 2004, the RIBA Drawings and Archives Collection. Until 1983 it was controlled directly by a government department; it is now a non-departmental public body, and entrance is free. Besides South Kensington it includes Young V&A, V&A Dundee, which opened in September 2018, and the V&A Wedgwood Collection, acquired in 2014.
victoriano-huerta: Huerta was born in Colotlán, Jalisco, to parents reported as ethnically Huichol, and identified himself as indigenous. He learned to read at the local priest's school, and chose a military career as the only way out of poverty. With the support of General Donato Guerra he entered the military academy at Chapultepec in 1872 and excelled at mathematics. Commissioned into the Corps of Engineers in 1877, he rose under the patronage of General Manuel González, and spent nine years on topographical surveys in Puebla and Veracruz. His hero was Napoleon, and he supported Porfirio Díaz as a strongman Mexico needed.

In 1911 he commanded the escort that took Díaz into exile. Under the interim president Francisco León de la Barra he fought Emiliano Zapata in Morelos, burning villages, which hindered Francisco I. Madero's later efforts at conciliation. In 1912 he defeated Pascual Orozco's rebellion at Rellano and became a national military hero.

In February 1913 a conspiracy of Félix Díaz, Bernardo Reyes and Manuel Mondragón began the Ten Tragic Days in Mexico City. Madero put Huerta in command, and Huerta secretly joined the plotters. The United States Ambassador, Henry Lane Wilson, took an active part, and the Embassy Pact provided for the exile of Madero and his vice president and for Huerta's takeover. Madero and José María Pino Suárez were seized on 18 February; Pedro Lascuráin held the presidency for under an hour and handed it to Huerta. Four days later Madero and Pino Suárez were shot by officers of the rurales, assumed to be acting on his orders.

The incoming Wilson administration in the United States refused to recognise the regime. Huerta suspended payment of the foreign debt, borrowed at a high rate and forced banks to issue paper money, which brought inflation. He resisted the United States landing at Veracruz in 1914, a stance even his opponents shared. The Constitutionalist Army won at the Battle of Zacatecas, and Huerta resigned in July 1914 and left for Spain, 17 months into his presidency.

Huerta reached the United States in April 1915 and dealt with the German naval agent Franz von Rintelen on a plan to regain power. He was arrested in June 1915 as he travelled to meet Orozco, held at Fort Bliss, and died in custody in January 1916, perhaps of cirrhosis or cancer; poisoning was widely suspected. Mexican historiography calls him the demon of the Revolution, and he is still known as El Chacal and El Usurpador.
vidin: Vidin lies on the southern bank of the Danube in north-western Bulgaria, close to the borders with Romania and Serbia. It is the westernmost important Bulgarian Danube port, and its hinterland is fertile and known for its wines. The town grew on the site of an old Celtic settlement called Dunonia, a name meaning fortified hill. The Romans built a fort, Bononia, on the Danubian Limes, around which a town developed that became one of the important centres of the province of Upper Moesia. Slavs who settled there called it Badin or Bdin, the source of the modern name.

In the Middle Ages Vidin was a bishop's seat and the capital of a large province of the First Bulgarian Empire. Between 971 and 976 it was the centre of the possessions of the future emperor Samuil. In 1003 Basil II took it after an eight-month siege, thanks to the betrayal of the local bishop. Under the Second Bulgarian Empire its despots were influential and sometimes chosen as emperors, and the Shishman dynasty ruled it from the mid 13th century. Michael Shishman threw off Serbian overlordship and was chosen tsar in 1323. In 1365 Hungarian crusaders occupied the Tsardom of Vidin, until Vladislav I of Wallachia drove them out in 1369 and Vidin was returned to Ivan Stratsimir.

After the Ottomans took Vidin in 1396 they made it a sandjak. Austrian forces held it for nine months from October 1689 during the Great Turkish War, and many Muslim houses and shops were destroyed; of 3,000 buildings, only 200 to 300 survived. Late in Ottoman rule Osman Pazvantoğlu's breakaway state centred on it. Vidin joined the Principality of Bulgaria after the liberation of 1878, and Serbian armies besieged it unsuccessfully in 1885 and 1913.

Vidin keeps two medieval fortresses, Baba Vida, built between the 10th and 14th centuries, and Kaleto. Its other monuments include the Orthodox churches of St Pantaleimon and St Petka, both of the 17th century, the Vidin Synagogue of 1894 and the Osman Pazvantoğlu Mosque and library. The theatre of 1891 was the first Bulgarian theatre in a European model. The New Europe Bridge, finished in 2013, joins the town to Calafat in Romania, replacing a ferry. Nearby are the Belogradchik Rocks and the Magura Cave with prehistoric paintings.
vidisha: Vidisha lies in the eastern Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh, 62.5 km northeast of the state capital Bhopal, in the fork of the Betwa and Bes rivers, about 9 km from Sanchi. The surrounding land has fertile black soil and low hills. The city was formerly known as Bhelsa, Besnagar and Bhaddalpur, and was renamed Vidisha in 1956. Its name is said to derive from the nearby river Bes, mentioned in the Puranas, and the Ramayana refers to Vidisha under the rule of Shatrughna, the youngest brother of Rama.

Besnagar, 3 km from the present city on the west side of the river, became an important trade centre in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE and is mentioned in the Pali scriptures. It flourished under the Shungas, Nagas, Satavahanas and Guptas. Ashoka was governor of Vidisha during his father's lifetime, and Ceylonese chronicles say his first wife, Devi, was the daughter of a merchant of Vedisagiri. The Heliodorus Pillar was erected by Heliodorus, ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, in the court of Bhagabhadra, in front of a temple of Vāsudeva. Its Brahmi inscription dedicates it as a Garuda standard to Vāsudeva.

In the medieval period Besnagar was called Bhelsa and became known for the temple of the sun god Bhillasvamin, first named in an inscription of 878 CE. Iltutmish is said to have destroyed the temple in the 1230s. Alauddin Khalji sacked the city in 1293 and Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1532, after which it passed to the Malwa Sultans, the Mughals and the Scindias. Under British rule it lay in the princely state of Gwalior, and the Quit India Movement in Madhya Pradesh began there in August 1942.

Vidisha is the administrative headquarters of Vidisha district and a Jain pilgrimage centre; Bhaddalpur is believed to be the birthplace of Shitalanatha, the tenth tirthankar. Its monuments include the Heliodorus Pillar, known locally as Kham Baba, the remains of the Bijamaṇḍal temple of the late Paramara period, and the tomb of Lohangi Pir. The 2011 census counted 155,951 inhabitants. Agriculture is the main economic activity.
vidkun-quisling: Quisling was born in Fyresdal, in Telemark, the son of the pastor and genealogist Jon Lauritz Qvisling and Anna Caroline Bang, daughter of a Grimstad ship-owner. He first came to international prominence as a close collaborator of the explorer Fridtjof Nansen. In January 1922 he arrived in Kharkiv to help the League of Nations relief effort during the Russian famine, and his report on the mismanagement and a death toll of about ten thousand a day attracted aid. He later served as a Norwegian diplomat in the Soviet Union, where he also managed British diplomatic affairs for a time. He returned to Norway in December 1929 with a plan called Norsk Aktion, which proposed radical constitutional change.

Quisling was defence minister in the Agrarian governments of Peder Kolstad and Jens Hundseid from 1931 to 1933, though he was neither an Agrarian nor a friend of Kolstad. In 1933 he founded the fascist Nasjonal Samling, or National Gathering. He gained some popularity through attacks on the political left, but the party won no seats in the Storting. In the summer of 1935 he told opponents that heads would roll once he achieved power, which damaged the party's image, and several high-ranking members, including his brother Jørgen, resigned. In 1939 he supported Hitler and toured German and Danish cities, where he was well received.

During the German invasion on 9 April 1940 Quisling attempted the first radio-broadcast coup d'état, but the Germans sought instead to persuade the recognised government to legitimise the occupation. Hitler appointed Josef Terboven Reichskommissar on 24 April, and Terboven forced Quisling to step down as party leader in June. After Quisling won Hitler over on 16 August, he formed a second government on 1 February 1942 as minister president, alongside Terboven's administration. On 12 March 1942 Norway officially became a one-party state, and criticism of the party was criminalised. His collaborationist government took part in Germany's war effort and deported Jews to concentration camps in occupied Poland.

Quisling turned himself in on 9 May 1945, and his trial opened on 20 August. He was found guilty of charges including embezzlement, murder and high treason, and was executed by firing squad at Akershus Fortress on 24 October 1945. Some criticised the sentence's legality, since no death sentence had been carried out in Norway since 1876. Nasjonal Samling was wiped out as a political force after 1945. The word quisling, coined by The Times in a leading article of 15 April 1940, became a synonym for traitor in several North European languages.
vidzeme: Vidzeme is one of the Historical Latvian Lands. Its name means the Middle Land, and in Old Latvian orthography it was written Widda-semme. It lies in north-central Latvia, north of the Daugava River, with the Latvian capital Riga in its south-western part. In German it was sometimes called Livland, from the Latin Livonia. Most of its inhabitants are Latvians, and it is the most ethnically Latvian region of the country.

In ancient times the territory was inhabited by Latgalians and by Livs, who lived near the coast of the Gulf of Riga and along the lower Daugava and Gauja rivers. Until the German conquest of the 13th century the Daugava marked the boundary between the lands of the Livs and Latgalians on its right bank and those of the Semigallians and Selonians on its left. The most notable Latgalian region in today's Vidzeme was Tālava.

After the Livonian War, part of the Livonian Confederation on the right bank of the Daugava and the Patrimony of Riga passed to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth as the Duchy of Livonia. Sweden invaded the region in 1600, 1617 and 1621. After the Truce of Altmark in 1629 Sweden acquired the western part of the Duchy of Livonia, roughly as far as the Aiviekste River, which has since formed Vidzeme's eastern border. Russia conquered Swedish Livonia in the Great Northern War and received it at the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. It created the Riga Governorate, renamed the Governorate of Livonia in 1796, which the local German Baltic nobility administered autonomously through a feudal Landtag.

After World War I the governorate was split between the newly independent Latvia and Estonia. The Soviet Union occupied Vidzeme from 1940, and Nazi Germany from 1941 to 1944. With the dissolution of the Soviet Union it became part of independent Latvia once more. Vidzeme is not an administrative unit, but Latvian law defines its territory by municipalities, among them Cēsis, Sigulda, Valmiera and Riga.
vienna: Vienna lies in north-eastern Austria at the easternmost extension of the Alps, on the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods and at the transition to the Pannonian Basin. The earliest settlement, on the site of the inner city, lay south of the meandering Danube, and the city now spans both banks. It is both a city and one of the nine states of Austria. The name is a Latinised form of the German Wien, which comes from the River Wien and first appears in the Salzburg Annals, recording a battle at a place called Wenia in 881.

In the 1st century the Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona, in the province of Pannonia, near the Danube to secure the frontier. Construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and the settlement at its peak had about 15,000 people. The emperor Marcus Aurelius may have died here in 180. The city was rebuilt after a Germanic invasion and served as a seat of Roman government until the fifth century, when its people fled the Huns and the site was abandoned for several centuries.

In 1155 Vienna became the seat of the Babenbergs, who ruled Austria from 976 to 1246, and in 1221 it was granted city rights. In the 16th century the Habsburgs made it the seat of the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire, which it remained until the empire's dissolution in 1806, with only a brief interruption. With the formation of the Austrian Empire in 1804 it became the capital of that empire and of all its successor states.

As capital of Austria-Hungary from 1867 to 1918 it grew sharply, and in 1910 it had more than two million inhabitants and was the third-largest city in Europe after London and Paris. Under the Nazi regime 65,000 Jews were deported from Vienna and murdered, and about 130,000 fled.

Vienna is the capital and most populous city of Austria, with just over two million inhabitants. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and includes Baroque palaces and gardens and the Ringstrasse of the late 19th century. Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert and Brahms were among the composers who worked there, and Sigmund Freud, the first psychoanalyst, lived there too. Since 1980 the city has been a United Nations headquarters city.
vienna-secession: The Vienna Secession, also called the Union of Austrian Artists, was founded on 3 April 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann, Joseph Maria Olbrich and others, who resigned from the Association of Austrian Artists, the Künstlerhaus, in protest against its support for traditional styles. Otto Wagner joined shortly afterwards. The name came from the Munich Secession of 1892. Its stated aims included contact with artists outside Austria, opposition to artistic nationalism, renewal of the decorative arts and a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total art uniting painting, architecture and the decorative arts. The group began with fifty members and elected Klimt its president, with Rudolf von Alt, aged eighty-five, as honorary president.

Olbrich's domed exhibition building of 1897 to 1898, with a frieze over the entrance, became the symbol of the movement and was the first dedicated gallery of contemporary art in Vienna. Between 1899 and 1903 it showed works by Monet, Degas, Renoir and other French artists. The 14th exhibition in 1902, designed by Hoffmann, was dedicated to Beethoven, with a statue by Max Klinger and Klimt's Beethoven Frieze. The group's magazine was Ver Sacrum.

Disputes arose after Hoffmann and Moser founded the Wiener Werkstätte in 1903. Members divided between those who put painting first and those who wanted equal treatment for the decorative arts. When a proposal to buy the Galerie Miethke was lost by one vote, Klimt, Hoffmann, Moser and others resigned on 14 June 1905, and Klimt formed the Kunstschau in 1906.

The Secession continued to hold exhibitions after 1905. Its building was destroyed under the Nazi regime as a symbol of degenerate art and rebuilt after the Second World War; Hoffmann rejoined in 1945 and was president from 1948 to 1950. Wagner's later work, such as the Austrian Postal Savings Bank of 1903 to 1906, and Hoffmann's Stoclet Palace in Brussels moved away from floral Art Nouveau towards geometric forms and the beginnings of modernism. Art Nouveau is named after the Vienna Secession in several languages of the former Austro-Hungary, such as Polish secesja and Czech secese, and the movement influenced Młoda Polska.
viet-cong: Viet Cong is a contraction of Việt Nam cộng sản, meaning Vietnamese communist, a term that acquired a derogatory sense by the late 1940s. After the Geneva Accords of 1954 about 90,000 Viet Minh were evacuated to the North, while 5,000 to 10,000 cadres stayed in the South. Ngo Dinh Diem announced in July 1955 that the election on reunification would not be held, and within a few months his campaign had driven the communists into remote swamps. An assassination campaign began in April 1957.

The Communist Party of Vietnam approved a people's war on the South in January 1959, and Group 559 was set up in May to maintain the Ho Chi Minh trail. The National Liberation Front was created on 20 December 1960 at Tân Lập village in Tây Ninh Province as a united front meant to draw in non-communists. Many core members were southern Viet Minh regroupees trained in the North.

The movement grew quickly: an estimated 300,000 members were enrolled in affiliated associations by early 1962, and its first victory over South Vietnamese forces came at Ấp Bắc in January 1963. It used guerrilla and regular units together with a network of cadres. It also used terror as a standard tactic, and death squads killed at least 37,000 civilians, according to the data available, which mostly cover 1967 to 1972.

In January and February 1968 some 80,000 fighters struck more than 100 towns in the Tet Offensive, including a raid on the United States embassy in Saigon and a massacre of about 3,500 residents at Huế. The hoped-for uprising did not come, and the offensive cost the movement heavily; Trần Văn Trà said about 75,000 were killed or wounded. In June 1969 the front and an urban alliance were merged into the Provisional Revolutionary Government.

After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 the Provisional Revolutionary Government moved into government offices, but authority over the South was given to the People's Army of Vietnam. People tainted by association with the old government were sent to re-education camps despite protests from non-communist members. The front and the alliance were later merged into the Vietnam Fatherland Front.

Its character was disputed. Opponents of American involvement said it was an insurgency native to the South, with chairman Nguyễn Hữu Thọ not a communist. Anti-communists said it was a front for Hanoi, and Trà's memoirs record that he followed orders from the party's military commission in Hanoi.
viet-minh: The Viet Minh, officially the League for Independence of Vietnam, was founded on 19 May 1941 at Pác Bó in Cao Bằng province by Ho Chi Minh. The Indochinese Communist Party set it up as a united front to achieve independence, the first step in a communist revolutionary project, and presented it as a broad coalition. Võ Nguyên Giáp commanded its military side, and Lê Duẩn and Phạm Văn Đồng were among the other founders. Non-communists also joined, including the Democratic Party and the Socialist Party, as did most Buddhists. Many Catholics, Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo followers first supported it but later split.

During the Second World War the Viet Minh fought the Japanese occupiers with support from the Republic of China and later the American Office of Strategic Services. At the end of 1944 it claimed 500,000 members. After the collapse of Japanese authority and the abdication of Emperor Bảo Đại, Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945. French and British forces attacked in the south from 23 September, and talks with France broke down in December 1946, leading to nearly ten years of war.

The French pushed the Viet Minh out of Hanoi, but their encirclement of the Việt Bắc base in late 1947 failed to defeat it. In 1950 the newly communist People's Republic of China provided bases and heavy weapons, and the Viet Minh took control of many rural areas. On 7 March 1951 it merged with the National United League of Vietnam to form the Vietnamese United Front, which people still called the Viet Minh.

After its victory at Điện Biên Phủ, France entered negotiations, and the Geneva Conference divided Vietnam at the 17th Parallel, with the Viet Minh army withdrawing to the North. Civil administration of North Vietnam passed to it on 11 October 1954, and Ho Chi Minh became prime minister. The promised unification elections of 1956 never took place, and Viet Minh cadres left in the South later took up an insurgency.

The United Front became the Vietnam Fatherland Front on 10 September 1955, today regarded as the modern incarnation of the Viet Minh. Its Vietnam Liberation Army, founded in 1944, is today the People's Army of Vietnam. Cambodian and Laotian movements, among them the Khmer Việt Minh and the Pathet Lao, received training and support from it.
vietnam: Vietnam lies on the eastern Indochinese Peninsula, with a total area of about 331,000 square kilometres, a coastline 3,444 kilometres long and land boundaries of 4,639 kilometres. At its narrowest point, in Quảng Trị province, it is as little as 50 kilometres across, and in the north it widens to around 600 kilometres.

The land is mostly hilly and densely forested, with level land covering no more than 20%. The Red River flows past Hanoi into the Gulf of Tonkin, and its delta, a plain of 15,000 square kilometres, has the highest population density of any region; its sediment advances the delta 60 to 80 metres into the South China Sea every year.

Humans lived in what is now Vietnam as early as the Paleolithic, and Homo erectus fossils dating to around 500,000 BCE have been found in caves in the north. By about 1,000 BCE wet-rice cultivation in the Ma River and Red River floodplains led to the Đông Sơn culture, known for its bronze casting and elaborate bronze drums.

Vietnamese legends hold that the Hồng Bàng dynasty of the Hùng kings, first established in 2879 BCE, was the first state, known as Văn Lang. In 257 BCE the last Hùng king was defeated by Thục Phán, who formed Âu Lạc and proclaimed himself An Dương Vương. The Han dynasty annexed northern and central Vietnam, which were then under Chinese rule from 111 BCE until the first dynasty emerged in 939.

Successive monarchical dynasties absorbed Chinese influences through Confucianism and Buddhism and expanded southward to the Mekong Delta, conquering Champa. During most of the 17th and 18th centuries Vietnam was effectively divided into two domains, Đàng Trong and Đàng Ngoài. The Nguyễn, the last imperial dynasty, surrendered to France in 1883, and in 1887 the territory was integrated into French Indochina as three separate regions. The Viet Minh launched the August Revolution and declared independence in 1945. France returned and was defeated in the First Indochina War in 1954, after which Vietnam was divided into two parts.

The Vietnam War was fought between communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and anti-communist South Vietnam, supported by the United States. After the North Vietnamese victory in 1975 the country reunified as a communist state under the Communist Party of Vietnam. An ineffective planned economy, a Western trade embargo and wars with Cambodia and China crippled it further, and in 1986 the party launched the Đổi Mới reforms toward a socialist-oriented market economy. Vietnam joined the World Trade Organization in 2007. Its population was 96,208,984 in the 2019 census; the Kinh make up 85.32% of it, and 54 ethnic groups are officially recognised.
vietnam-war: Vietnam had been under French control as part of French Indochina since the 1880s. After the French defeat in the First Indochina War, Vietnam's independence was affirmed at the 1954 Geneva Conference, which divided the country at the 17th parallel. The communists under Ho Chi Minh took power in North Vietnam, while an anticommunist regime under Ngô Đình Diệm took control of South Vietnam with United States backing. The North Vietnamese supplied and eventually directed the Viet Cong, a communist front in the south that intensified a guerrilla war from 1957. The war was at once a postcolonial war of national liberation, a theatre of the Cold War and a civil war. In 1963 Diệm was killed in a US-backed military coup.

After the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964, the US Congress passed a resolution that gave President Lyndon B. Johnson authority to increase the military presence without declaring war. On 8 March 1965, 3,500 US Marines landed near Da Nang, the start of the ground war, and deployment rose to 536,000 by 1969. The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a tactical defeat for the communists but contributed to growing American opposition to the war. Richard Nixon began Vietnamization from 1969, in which an expanded South Vietnamese army took over the fighting as US forces withdrew. Fighting spilled into Laos and Cambodia.

After the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 the last American forces left, but fighting continued. In March 1975 North Vietnamese forces opened an offensive in the Central Highlands, and the South Vietnamese army collapsed. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, after the largest helicopter evacuation in history, Operation Frequent Wind.

North and South Vietnam were merged in July 1976 as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Estimates of the dead vary widely. About 58,220 US service members died, and estimates run from 275,000 to 310,000 Cambodians and 20,000 to 62,000 Laotians. The war was marked by atrocities, among them the massacres at Huế and Mỹ Lai, and some 20 percent of South Vietnam's jungle was sprayed with toxic herbicides, which led to significant health problems. Political repression and flawed economic policies after the war precipitated the flight of the Vietnamese boat people, of whom about 250,000 perished at sea. In the United States the war gave rise to Vietnam syndrome, an aversion to overseas military involvement.
vijayanagara-empire: Before the empire's rise, the Seunas of Devagiri, the Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal, the Pandyan Empire of Madurai and the Hoysalas of Belur had all been raided or annexed by the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq. The short-lived Kampili kingdom in the Tungabhadra basin fell to Tughluq forces around 1327 to 1328. The brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty founded the kingdom in 1336. By 1374 Bukka Raya I had defeated the chiefdom of Arcot, the Reddys of Kondavidu and the Sultan of Madurai, and held Goa and the Tungabhadra-Krishna doab.

The empire reached its peak under Krishna Deva Raya (1509 to 1529), who took Raichur in 1520 and Gulbarga from the Deccan sultanates and won the Kalinga region from the Gajapatis of Odisha. After the death of Achyuta Deva Raya in June 1542, the regent Salakaraju Tirumala seized power, had the boy Venkata I killed and invited the Sultan of Bijapur to sit on the throne symbolically. The nobility's anger began a civil war in 1542 to 1543. In January 1565 the united Deccan sultanates defeated Rama Raya's army at the Battle of Talikota, though the empire lasted until 1646.

The emperor was assisted by a cabinet of ministers headed by a prime minister, the Mahapradhana, and all high officers had military training. The economy rested on agriculture: cotton fed a large textile industry, betel, areca and coconut were the chief cash crops, and spices came from the Malnad hills. The capital was a centre of trade in gems and gold, and temple building employed thousands of masons and sculptors.

The founders were devout Shaivas who also made grants to Vishnu temples, and the later Saluva and Tuluva kings were Vaishnava by faith. Visitors recorded that the emperors tolerated all religions. Administration and court used Kannada, while Telugu gained literary prominence under the last emperors, especially Krishnadevaraya. At the Mahanavami festival the king received gifts and tribute from subordinate rulers and reviewed their armies on the last day.

The capital's ruins near modern Hampi are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Vijayanagara architecture combined Chalukya, Hoysala, Pandya and Chola forms, with tall gateway towers called rajagopurams and pillared halls, built in hard local granite. Carnatic music took its classical structure in this era. The Mahanavami ceremonies passed to successor states, and Raja Wodeyar I held Dasara at Srirangapatna in 1610, from which the modern Mysore Dasara developed. Knowledge of the empire rests on inscriptions, excavations and the accounts of visitors such as Domingo Paes, Fernão Nunes, Niccolò de' Conti and Abdul Razzaq.
vijayawada: Vijayawada lies on the banks of the Krishna River at an altitude of 11 m (36 ft) above sea level, flanked by the Eastern Ghats and the Indrakeeladri Hills. Three canals that leave the north side of the reservoir behind the Prakasam Barrage, the Eluru, Bandar and Ryves canals, flow through the city. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with the hottest weather in May and the coolest in January, and rain from both the south-west and north-east monsoons.

The name is explained by several legends. In one, the goddess Durga killed the demon Mahishasura and rested here, so that the place became the land of victory, from vijaya, victory, and wada, place. In another, the hero Arjuna of the Mahabharata prayed on the Indrakeeladri hill and received the weapon Pashupatastra from Shiva; one of Arjuna's names is Vijaya. The place was called Vijayavatika before it became Vijayawada.

Bezawada, as the city was then known, is said to have been founded around 626 CE by the Paricchedi kings, and it was ruled by Madhava Varma, one of the kings of the Vishnukundina dynasty. The Chinese Buddhist scholar Xuanzang stayed there for a few years around 640 CE to copy and study the Abhidhamma Pitaka, the last of the three baskets of the Pali canon, the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism.

The Mogalrajapuram hills hold five rock-cut temples built between the fourth and ninth centuries, and some of the caves can be attributed to the Vishnukundina dynasty.
