The Akkana Madanna Caves at the foot of Indrakeeladri Hill are a monument of national importance. In the modern period the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation was constituted on 1 April 1888, the same year the Vijayawada Junction railway station was established, and a line to Hyderabad was laid in 1889. Andhra Cements, founded in 1937, was the first cement factory in Andhra Pradesh.

Vijayawada is the second most populous city of Andhra Pradesh, with 1,021,806 people at the 2011 census, most of them Telugu speakers and Hindus, with Muslim, Christian and Jain minorities. It is a trading centre, notable for the mango market at Nunna, and an important rail and road junction. Its Hindu festivals include Durga Pooja and a boat festival, the Theppotsavam, on the Krishna during Dussera, centred on the Kanaka Durga Temple on Indrakeeladri hill. Kondapalli toys, handmade wooden toys from a suburb of the city, received a geographical indication in 2007.
viking-age: Many theories are put forward for the Viking expansion, and the will to explore likely played a major role. England, Wales and Ireland were divided into warring kingdoms and vulnerable, while the Franks were well defended. Overpopulation is one proposed cause, though some scholars reject it. Others point to growing urbanism and trade, as wealth moving along the routes of the expanding Islamic world drew Scandinavians to rich towns such as the wich towns of Anglo-Saxon England. Political centralisation in Scandinavia, especially in Norway, may have pushed people out, and advances in sailing, including larger sails, tacking and round-the-clock voyages, made distant targets possible.

The best-known beginning is the attack of 8 June 793 that destroyed the abbey on Lindisfarne, though Judith Jesch has argued that the age began between 700 and 750, since earlier contacts are likely. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle also records three Norwegian boats landing at Portland in 789.

Voyaging from Denmark, Norway and Sweden, Norse people settled in the British Isles, Ireland, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy and the Baltic coast, and briefly in Newfoundland. In the east they travelled along the Dnieper and Volga routes, where they were known as Varangians. They raided Iona in 794 and monasteries in Gaelic Ireland from 795, and from 840 built fortified camps called longphorts, the first at Dublin and Linn Duachaill. Their kingdoms and earldoms included the Kingdom of the Isles, Orkney, York, the Danelaw, Dublin, Normandy and Kievan Rus'.

In 844 a fleet appeared at the mouth of the Tagus, and in 959 an expedition under Björn Ironside and Hásteinn burned the mosque at Seville. In the 11th century the Norse homelands were unified into larger kingdoms.

Most of the age was pagan, and Scandinavia was Christianised towards its later part, with early centres in Denmark. Longships and the broader knarr, used for trade, gave the Norse a formidable reputation. Important trading ports included Ribe, Hedeby, Kaupang, Birka and Dublin.

The Icelandic sagas are seen as characteristic works of the time, and Old Norse shaped later languages. More than a thousand Old Norse words entered Standard English, among them sky, skin, window, law and sister, and many place names in eastern and north-eastern England are Danish.
vikings: The Viking Age is taken to run from the earliest recorded raid by Norsemen in 793 to the Norman conquest of England in 1066. In England it began on 8 June 793, when Norsemen destroyed the abbey on the island of Lindisfarne. The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York declared that never before had such an atrocity been seen, and medieval Christians could find no explanation for the suffering save the wrath of God.

The Vikings raided, traded, acted as mercenaries and settled over a wide area. Early raiders probably returned home, but later Vikings settled in the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy and the Baltic coast, and along the Dnieper and Volga routes, where they were known as Varangians. Vikings under Leif Erikson reached North America and set up short-lived settlements at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Two Vikings ruled England: Sweyn Forkbeard claimed the throne from 1013 to 1014, and his son Cnut the Great was king from 1016 to 1035. By the late 11th century the Church was legitimising royal dynasties, and the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden were taking shape.

Viking society was divided into thralls, karls and jarls, a structure described in the Eddic poem Rígsþula and confirmed by archaeology. Most Vikings were farmers, fishermen, craftsmen and traders. They spoke Old Norse and wrote inscriptions in runes, usually short and formulaic, so most contemporary written sources come from Christian and Islamic communities outside Scandinavia, often by authors who had suffered from Viking activity. They followed the Old Norse religion for most of the period and became Christians over the 8th to 12th centuries.

Their longships had a long, narrow hull and shallow draught, with oars to complement the sail, which let crews land in shallow water. Scandinavia used little coinage outside trading centres such as Ribe and Hedeby, so exchange rested on the weight and purity of silver, measured with small portable scales.

The Vikings influenced Old English, and so Modern English. The Normans descended from Vikings given overlordship of the Duchy of Normandy in the 10th century. Not until the 1890s did scholars outside Scandinavia begin to reassess Viking artistry, technology and seamanship. There is no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets, a costume element that first appeared in the 19th century.
vikram-samvat: According to popular tradition, King Vikramaditya of Ujjain established the era after defeating the Śakas. The Jain text Kalakacharya Kathanaka tells that King Gandharvasena of Ujjain abducted a nun, Sarasvati, sister of the monk Kalakacharya. The monk sought help from the Śaka ruler in Sistan, who defeated Gandharvasena. The defeated king's son Vikramaditya later drove the Śakas from Ujjain and began a new era to mark the event. Colonial scholarship accepted this theory, but later inscriptions and study suggest it has no historical basis.

The era beginning in 57 BCE was first known by other names: Krita in inscriptions of 343 and 371, the era of the Malava tribe in 424, or simply Samvat. The earliest inscription calling it Vikrama is from 842, found at Dholpur and dated 20 April 842. The earliest to link it with a king named Vikramaditya dates from 971. Some authors hold that Vikramaditya was a figure of tradition or a title taken by a later king, such as Chandragupta II or Yashodharman, who renamed the era.

Vikram Samvat is lunisolar, like the Hebrew and Chinese calendars. A common lunar year has 354 days, and a leap month, the adhika masa, is added roughly seven times every 19 years so that festivals and crop rituals stay in season. Each month has two fortnights: the waxing, bright shukla paksha and the waning, dark krishna paksha. Days are counted in tithis, each the time the angle between the Moon and the Sun grows by 12 degrees. The year count is usually 57 ahead of the Gregorian one, and 56 ahead from January to March or April.

Hindus, Sikhs and Pashtuns have used the calendar. In north India the lunar year begins with the new moon of Chaitra, the beginning of Chaitra Navaratri, while Vaisakhi marks the solar new year in Punjab and other regions, and in Gujarat the new year falls on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kartika. Under Islamic rule the Hijri calendar became official, and under British rule the Gregorian calendar was adopted. Buddhist and Jain inscriptions continued to use eras based on the Buddha or Mahavira.

The Rana dynasty of Nepal made Vikram Samvat the official calendar in 1901, which began as 1958 VS. Nepal's new year starts on the first day of Baisakh, around 13 to 15 April, and is a public holiday. In India the reformed Saka calendar is the official one, except for traditional festival dates; the Hindi preamble of the Indian constitution dates its adoption of 26 November 1949 as Samvat 2006.
vikramaditya-i: Vikramaditya was one of several sons of Pulakeshin II; the later Chalukyas of Kalyani made him a son of Pulakeshin's son Adityavarman, a statement that can be dismissed as inaccurate. Pulakeshin was defeated and probably killed when the Pallavas invaded Vatapi around 642, and the history of the next decade is unclear. The throne may have passed to Adityavarman, his son Abhinavaditya and then another brother, Chandraditya, whose widow Vijaya-Bhattarika appears to have acted as regent for their minor son.

During that regency Vikramaditya seems to have risen as supreme commander of the army and ruler in practice. His inscriptions say that he recovered the regal fortune of his father, which had been concealed by three kings. The historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri took these to include his brothers and supposed a partition of the kingdom, but there is no evidence of one; D. C. Sircar and others hold that he fought the Pallavas as a subordinate of his brothers and took the throne only after their deaths. His Gadval inscription of about 674, dated to his twelfth regnal year, places his accession about 655.

With the help of his maternal grandfather, a king of the Western Ganga dynasty, Vikramaditya ended a Pallava occupation that had lasted thirteen years. He gave his loyal younger brother Jayasimhavarma the viceroyalty of Lata in southern Gujarat. Against the Pallava kings Mahendravarman II and Paramesvaravarman I he allied himself with the Pandyas, and by 670 he had a military camp at Malliyur, west of Kanchipuram. Chalukya records claim that he defeated Paramesvaravarman I and took Kanchi but did not destroy it; the writer Anirudh Kanisetti holds that the city was sacked.

Chalukya records place him in camp at Uragapura on the south bank of the Kaveri river on 25 April 674. At Peruvalanallur he met Paramesvaravarman I and a Pandya king, and Pallava and Pandya records alike claim that the Chalukyas were defeated there. Pallava inscriptions also speak of the destruction of the city of Ranarasika, an epithet of Vikramaditya, but several historians question whether Vatapi was sacked a second time; Chalukya records credit his son Vinayaditya and grandson Vijayaditya with defeating the invaders.

Vikramaditya bore titles that advertised his military power, among them Rana-rasika, lover of war, Anivarita, unopposed, and Raja-malla, royal wrestler. He was married to the Western Ganga princess Gangamahadevi. Under him the Chalukya kingdom recovered most of the territory it had controlled under Pulakeshin II. He died in 680 and was succeeded by his son Vinayaditya.
vila-velha: Vila Velha, whose name means Old Village, lies on the Atlantic coast of the state of Espírito Santo in south-eastern Brazil, about 10 km south of the state capital, Vitória, with which it forms part of the Greater Vitória Metropolitan Area.

The terrain is mostly flat, the municipal seat standing about 4 m above sea level, and the 32 km of coastline is almost entirely lined with beaches. Several hills rise from the plain, among them Morro da Penha at 154 m, which carries the Penha Convent, and Morro do Moreno at 164 m, which preserves a remnant of the Atlantic Forest, the original vegetation of the area.

In the 16th century the area was contested by three Indigenous groups: the Goitacá from the south, the Aimoré from the interior and the Tupiniquim from the north. On 23 May 1535 the Portuguese Vasco Fernandes Coutinho, grantee of the Captaincy of Espírito Santo, landed at the present-day Prainha, which the Indigenous people called Piratininga, from the caravel Glória with 60 men. He founded the Vila do Espírito Santo, now Vila Velha, so named because it was the Sunday of Pentecost. The settlement became the captaincy's capital, and the seat was later transferred to Vitória.

Agriculture sustained the town for much of its history and declined in the 20th century, giving way to commerce, tourism and industry. The chocolate factory Garoto was founded there in August 1929. The port terminal is one of the largest in south-eastern Brazil. Theatre has been part of the town since the colonial period: plays written by Jesuits were performed in the late 16th century, among them Na Visitação de Santa Izabel of 1597 by Father Joseph of Anchieta.

Vila Velha is the oldest city in the state and holds several historic landmarks, including the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary, the Fort of São Francisco Xavier de Piratininga and the Santa Luzia Lighthouse. The Penha Convent, one of the oldest churches in Espírito Santo, was begun around 1558 under Friar Pedro Palácios and was designated a national cultural heritage site by the heritage institute Iphan in 1943.
Its high altar, built around 1800 in the Rococo style, has over 200 pieces of 19 types of marble. The city has about half a million inhabitants, and its anniversary on 23 May is also a state holiday.
viljandi: Viljandi lies on the north-western shore of Lake Viljandi, in a primeval valley, between the Estonian cities of Pärnu and Tartu. It is the capital of Viljandi County. Its symbol is a white rose, and 720 white roses were planted before the city hall for the anniversary in 2003. The first records of settlement near the town date to the fifth millennium BCE, and the earthen stronghold is first mentioned in 1154 in the commentaries to al-Idrisi's world atlas Geography.

In the twelfth century a permanent settlement emerged around the stronghold, which became the economic centre of the ancient Sakala district. In 1211 the hillfort of the Estonians was besieged by a joint army of Germans, Latvians and Livonians. The Livonian Sword Brethren, later the Livonian Order, started a powerful Order centre in place of the wooden stronghold in 1224, and the following year Grand Master Volquin led the building of Viljandi Castle on the site of the hillfort. It was one of the largest castles of the Baltic region, a commander was appointed to it from 1248, and it was rebuilt and modernised over the next two hundred years.

In the thirteenth century a medieval town arose on the north side of the stronghold, with the Hamburg-Riga town bylaws, first recorded in 1283. In the first half of the fourteenth century Viljandi joined the Hanseatic League, as an important stop for merchants travelling to and from Russia. In 1481 Ivan III of Russia besieged the castle but could not take it. The decline began in the Livonian War, and in 1560 the forces of Knyaz Andrey Kurbsky of Muscovite Russia seized and demolished the town and the stronghold. They were destroyed again in the Polish–Russian War of the early seventeenth century, and under Swedish rule the town bylaws were cancelled. They were restored in 1783, when Catherine II's reforms made Viljandi a district town.

Viljandi has about 17,000 inhabitants. The ruins of the castle lie in a park, and the town belongs to the international city league the Hanse. It is sometimes called the cultural capital of Estonia, partly because of the Viljandi Culture Academy, and the Viljandi Folk Music Festival is held each summer. The newspaper Sakala was founded there in 1878, and the railway station opened in 1897.
villefranche-sur-mer: Villefranche-sur-Mer lies on the French Riviera, immediately east of Nice below Mont Boron, Mont Alban and Mont Vinaigrier. Its name means Free City on Sea in Old French. The bay is one of the deepest natural harbours of the Mediterranean, reaching 98 metres between the Cape of Nice and Cap Ferrat, and it gives safe anchorage to large ships in easterly winds. Offshore it extends into an undersea canyon. The town's limits climb the surrounding hills to 577 metres at Mont-Leuze.

The site has been settled since prehistoric times, when Celto-Ligurian tribes farmed the hills. The Greeks and later the Romans used the harbour as a stop on the way to settlements in the western Mediterranean, and after Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul the Romans extended the Via Aurelia through the settlement of Montolivo. In 1295 Charles II, Duke of Anjou and Count of Provence, persuaded the people of Montolivo and its surroundings to settle nearer the coast, to protect the area from pirates. He established Villefranche by charter as a free port, with tax privileges and port fee rights that lasted well into the 18th century.

By 1388 East Provence had passed to the Duchy of Savoy after the disputed succession to Queen Joan I of Naples. In 1543 Franco-Turkish armies sacked and occupied the town after the siege of Nice, and Duke Emmanuel Philibert then built a citadel, in 1557, and a fort on Mont Alban. French forces occupied the town again in 1793, and the county of Nice remained part of the Napoleonic Empire until 1814. It was given to France in 1860 by treaty after a plebiscite.

The citadel now houses the town hall, a convention centre, three museums and an open-air theatre. The old harbour of la Darse dates from the 17th century, when it was built for the galleys of the Duke of Savoy, and today it is a marina and the site of an oceanographic observatory. The Rue Obscure, a passage under the harbour-front houses, dates from 1260. The Chapelle Saint-Pierre, from the sixteenth century, was restored in 1957 with murals by Jean Cocteau. The United States Sixth Fleet had its home port at Villefranche from 1948 to 1966.
vilna-gaon: Elijah ben Solomon Zalman was born on 23 April 1720 in Sielec, then in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and now Syalyets in Belarus. His father was a rabbi. By nine he had begun to study Kabbalah, devoting several hours a day to the Zohar and the writings of Isaac Luria, and by ten he studied without teachers. By the age of twenty, rabbis were submitting their hardest legal problems to him. He married Chana, daughter of Yehuda Leib of Kaidan, who managed the household so that he could give himself wholly to study.

He wrote glosses on the Babylonian Talmud and the Shulchan Aruch, known as Bi'urei ha-Gra, a running commentary on the Mishnah, and commentaries on the Book of Proverbs and on Kabbalistic texts. None of his manuscripts was published in his lifetime. He favoured study of the literal meaning of a text and, like Maimonides, opposed pilpul, the sharp dialectical analysis of the schools. He often ruled according to his own reading of the Talmud, even against the Shulchan Aruch or established custom.

He supported secular studies that helped to understand the Torah. He wrote a book on mathematics, astronomy and geometry, Ayil Meshulash, and a Hebrew translation of Euclid's Elements was published in The Hague in 1780 with an introduction quoting his words. He condemned philosophy and metaphysics and opposed the study of the humanities in general. In Kabbalah he rejected the reception of revelations through a maggid, preferring to seek wisdom directly through study.

He held no official post and did not head a yeshiva. In the winter of 1767 he set up a beit midrash next to his home, where select scholars studied and brought him their questions. His students felt the gap between themselves and him so strongly that they refused to be called his students. The best known was Chaim of Volozhin, who founded the Volozhin Yeshiva and wrote Nefesh HaChaim, partly as a reply to Hasidism.

He opposed Hasidism, which he regarded as a deviation from the faith. His signature appears on the Vilna community's decree of excommunication against it in 1772, and he issued another in 1781. He refused to meet Shneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of the Chabad movement. Some of his followers later settled in Jerusalem. He died in Vilnius on 9 October 1797. In 2020, the 300th anniversary of his birth, the Lithuanian Parliament declared the Year of the Vilna Gaon.
vilnius: Vilnius lies at the confluence of the Vilnia and Neris rivers in southeastern Lithuania, 312 km from the Baltic Sea and the main Lithuanian seaport, Klaipėda. The city covers 402 km2, of which 68.8 per cent is green space. Its name comes from the river Vilnia, an old Lithuanian name meaning ripple, which was transferred to the city. The name first appears in Latin letters of Grand Duke Gediminas in 1323, in the form Vilna, and in 1325 as Wilno, a form still used in Polish. The Lithuanian form Vilnius was recorded around 1600 in the Postil of Mikalojus Daukša and became widespread during the national revival at the end of the 19th century.

The history of Vilnius goes back to the Stone Age. From at least 1323 until 1795 the city was the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and from the 13th century until the mid-17th century the Vilnius Castle Complex was the residence of the Lithuanian monarchs. Magdeburg rights were granted in 1378, and a magistrate or city council, subordinate to the ruler, then governed it.

In 1517 the Italian princess Bona Sforza married the Lithuanian Grand Duke Sigismund I the Old, which strengthened the Italian influence on the city's Renaissance and Baroque architecture. Vilnius became an artistic centre of the Grand Duchy, attracting artists from across Europe. Under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth it was noted for its multicultural population, which contemporary sources compared to Babylon. Before World War II and the Holocaust it was one of Europe's most important Jewish centres.

Later Vilnius was ruled by imperial and Soviet Russia, Napoleonic France, Imperial and Nazi Germany and interwar Poland, and it again became a capital of Lithuania in the 20th century. Before World War II Poles made up the majority of inhabitants, and the population exchange between Poland and Soviet Lithuania after the war changed that.

Vilnius is the capital and largest city of Lithuania and the most populous city in the Baltic states. Its Old Town, considered one of the largest and best-preserved in Europe, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. The Baroque style known as Vilnian Baroque is named after the city, which is the easternmost Baroque city and the largest north of the Alps. Around two thirds of its residents were Lithuanians in 2021.
vilnius-university: In 1568 the Lithuanian nobility asked the Jesuits to create an institution of higher learning in Vilnius or Kaunas. The following year Walerian Protasewicz, the bishop of Vilnius, bought several buildings in the city centre and established the college, which first enrolled students in 1570, 160 of them in its first year. A library was founded the same year, and Sigismund II Augustus donated 2,500 books to it.

Teaching was in Latin, in three divisions: humanities, philosophy and theology. The university was founded in 1579 as the Jesuit Academy of Vilnius by Stephen Báthory. It was the third oldest university, after the Cracow Academy and the Albertina, in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the only one in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

Vilnius University was prominent in the Baroque era. The Jesuits hired the architect Joannes Christophorus Glaubicius to repair its buildings and the Church of St. Johns, and he developed a Vilnius Baroque style. In 1753 Tomasz Żebrowski founded the first observatory in the Commonwealth, the fourth professional one in Europe.

In 1773 the Commission of National Education, the world's first ministry of education, took control of the academy and turned it into a modern university, and the language of teaching changed from Latin to Polish. After the failure of the November Uprising of 1830 to 1831 the university was closed and remained suspended until 1919, when it resumed as the Polish Stefan Batory University on 28 August with the authorisation of Józef Piłsudski.

In October 1939 Vilnius was transferred to Lithuania, and on 15 December the Lithuanian authorities closed the university and dismissed about 3,000 students. A new university named Vilniaus universitetas was created with Lithuanian as its language. Under the Nazi occupation all Jewish teachers and later all Polish and Jewish students were expelled, and nearly all the Jewish members of the university community became victims of the Holocaust. Under Soviet rule lecturers were arrested from 1945 until Stalin's death. On 12 June 1990 the Supreme Council of Lithuania approved a new statute declaring the university's autonomy.

The historic ensemble in the old town, with around thirteen courtyards, still serves its original educational role. The library, founded in 1570, is the earliest academic library in the Baltic region and holds over five million documents, including collections of old printed books and manuscripts, and its Central Library still works in its authentic 16th-century premises. The poet Czesław Miłosz, Nobel laureate in literature in 1980, was an alumnus.
vilshofen-an-der-donau: Vilshofen an der Donau lies at the confluence of the Vils, Pfudrach and Wolfach with the Danube, south of the Bavarian Forest, and is sometimes called the three-river town. Its height above sea level ranges from 309 to 457 metres. Here the Danube cut into the crystalline basement as the Bavarian Forest rose in the Late Tertiary and Quaternary, forming an impressive valley that continues far beyond Passau. Granite was quarried in the Vils valley nature reserve until the middle of the 20th century, and the abandoned quarries partly flooded, creating the Taferlsee.

The documented history of Vilshofen begins in 776, when a farm called Vilusa was donated to the Mondsee monastery. The Bishop of Passau was landlord of the Danube and Vils, and the Count of Ortenburg held Vilshofen as a fief. Count Heinrich I of Ortenburg raised it to a town in 1206, and a bridge over the Vils is reported in 1220. In 1241 Duke Otto II of Bavaria took the town by force after an inheritance dispute in the House of Ortenburg, making it a border town between Bavaria and the Prince-Bishopric of Passau. It finally passed to Bavaria in 1262 under a treaty negotiated by Duke Henry of Lower Bavaria with Bishop Rüdiger of Passau.

Emperor Ludwig the Bavarian confirmed the town charter in 1345, and a collegiate monastery was founded in 1376. The oldest town seal dates from 1434. In 1504 the town was defended successfully against attackers from the Palatinate and Bohemia in the Landshut War of Succession, and in 1536 a large fire destroyed 36 houses. Until 1972 Vilshofen was the seat of its own district.

Vilshofen is the largest town in the southeast of Bavaria and lies in the district of Passau, about 20 kilometres upstream of Passau. A Benedictine monastery was founded at Schweiklberg in 1904. The town lies on the Danube Cycle Path and is a port of call for river cruise vessels. In 2006 it marked the 800th anniversary of its elevation to a town. The brewer Josef Groll was born there in 1813.
vincent-auriol: Vincent Jules Auriol was born on 27 August 1884 in Revel, Haute-Garonne, the only child of a baker. He took a law degree and began work as a lawyer in Toulouse. A committed socialist, he co-founded the newspaper Le Midi Socialiste in 1908. In 1914 he entered the Chamber of Deputies as a Socialist for Muret, and he was mayor of Muret from 1925 to 1947. After the party split in December 1920, he refused to join the new SFIC and became, with Léon Blum, a leader of the remaining SFIO. He became its leading spokesman on financial questions, and he chaired the Finance Committee of the Chamber from 1924 to 1926.

As Minister of Finance in Blum's government of 1936–1937, Auriol devalued the franc by 30 per cent against the dollar, which led to capital flight. He was Minister of Justice in the next government, under Camille Chautemps. On 10 July 1940 he was one of the 80 deputies who voted against the extraordinary powers given to Philippe Pétain. He was placed under house arrest until he escaped to the Resistance in October 1942, and he reached London in October 1943. He represented the Socialists at the Free French Consultative Assembly and France at the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944. After the war he served in Charles de Gaulle's provisional government and presided over the Constituent Assemblies.

On 16 January 1947 the National Assembly elected Auriol the first President of the Fourth Republic, with 452 votes against 242 for Auguste Champetier de Ribes. His presidency was relatively weak, like the office under the Third Republic. Strikes in 1947 escalated into violence, and the government deployed 80,000 reservists. The war in Indochina and unrest in Morocco, Madagascar, Algeria and Tunisia marked the period. France joined the Council of Europe and NATO as a founding member, and the Monnet Plan was put into effect. Auriol did not seek re-election, and René Coty succeeded him on 16 January 1954. There had been eighteen governments in his seven years.
vincent-van-gogh: Vincent Willem van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert, in the predominantly Catholic province of North Brabant. He was the oldest surviving child of Theodorus van Gogh, a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church, and Anna Cornelia Carbentus. His grandfather, also named Vincent, was a prominent art dealer, and three of that grandfather's six sons became art dealers. His younger brother Theo was born on 1 May 1857. Van Gogh was taught at home, then sent to boarding school at Zevenbergen and in 1866 to the middle school in Tilburg, where he was deeply unhappy. He returned home in March 1868 and later wrote that his youth was "austere and cold, and sterile."

As an adult he began painting at an elementary level. In early 1882 his uncle Cornelis Marinus, owner of a gallery in Amsterdam, commissioned drawings of The Hague but was twice disappointed. Theo gave him money for materials in August 1882. From early 1883 Van Gogh worked on multi-figure compositions, and he destroyed several large paintings made at Nuenen; The Potato Eaters and its companion pieces are the only ones to survive. In November 1885 he travelled to Antwerp and later to Paris, where he met Émile Bernard and Paul Gauguin. His colours grew brighter, and his style was fully realised during his stay in Arles in 1888, when he painted series of olive trees, wheat fields and sunflowers.

The correspondence with Theo is the most comprehensive primary source on his work. It includes more than 600 letters from Vincent to Theo, and most of what is known of his theories of art is recorded in them.

Van Gogh suffered from psychotic episodes and delusions. His friendship with Gauguin ended after a confrontation with a razor, when he severed part of his own left ear. He spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including one at Saint-Rémy, and then moved to the Auberge Ravoux in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he came under the care of Dr Paul Gachet. On 27 July 1890 he shot himself in the chest and died two days later.

His reputation grew steadily among artists and critics after exhibitions in the late 1880s. Theo died in January 1891, and Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger took charge of the paintings and letters. Memorial exhibitions were held in several cities, and in 1896 the young Henri Matisse was introduced to Van Gogh's work and turned to bright colours. The Fauves and German Expressionists later took up elements of his style.
vindhya-range: The Vindhyas are not a single range in the geological sense: they are a discontinuous chain of ridges, hill ranges, highlands and plateau escarpments, and the term is defined by convention. Today it mainly means the escarpment and its hilly extensions north of the Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh, forming the southern wall of the Malwa plateau. Its western end lies in Gujarat, joined to the Aravalli Range near Champaner. In the east it divides into a southern chain meeting the Satpura Range in the Maikal Hills and a northern chain continuing as the Bhander Plateau and the Kaimur Range, with a branch across Bundelkhand known as the Panna range. It averages roughly 300 to 650 metres in height.

Older texts used the name more widely, for hills between the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Deccan, extending to the Godavari in the south and the Ganges in the north. Some Puranas apply it to what is now called the Satpura Range. Ancient texts mention three ranges in Central India, Vindhya, Rksa and Pariyatra, among the seven clan mountains of Bharatavarsha. The Greek geographer Ptolemy called the range Vindius or Ouindion and described it as the source of the Narmada and the Tapti.

Several ancient texts treat the Vindhyas as the southern boundary of Āryāvarta, and they remained the traditional dividing line between northern and southern India, though it is debated whether they marked a cultural boundary or only the southern limit of the settled societies then known. They were long considered inaccessible and dangerous because of dense vegetation and the tribes living there, and the Mahabharata places the Nishadas and other peoples in their forests. A legend tells that the mountain grew until it blocked the sun, and the sage Agastya asked it to lower itself so that he could cross south; it promised never to grow again.

Tributaries of the Ganga-Yamuna system, among them the Chambal, Betwa, Ken and Parbati, rise in the Vindhyas and drain their northern slopes, while the Narmada and Son drain the southern. Their highest point is Sad-bhawna Shikhar, 752 metres above sea level, in the Damoh district. A temple to Vindhyavasini, a fierce form of the goddess Shakti, stands at Vindhyachal in Uttar Pradesh. The Vindhyan Supergroup is one of the largest and thickest sedimentary successions in the world, and the Vindhya basin has yielded what may be the earliest known multicellular eukaryote fossils, perhaps 1.6 to 1.7 billion years old.
violeta-chamorro: Violeta Barrios Torres was born on 18 October 1929 in Rivas, near the Costa Rican border, into a wealthy and conservative family with large landholdings and cattle. She attended school in Rivas, Granada and Managua and then American schools in Texas and Virginia, returning home in June 1947 when her father was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. She met Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal in 1949, and they married in December 1950 and had five children. In 1952 he inherited the newspaper La Prensa, which became a voice of opposition to the Somoza regime, and he was frequently jailed or exiled; she followed him abroad or visited him in jail for about a decade.

After her husband's assassination in 1978 she took over La Prensa. When Daniel Ortega led the Sandinista guerrillas into Managua in July 1979, she was with them and represented the Democratic Union of Liberation on the Junta of National Reconstruction. She resigned on 19 April 1980, when the junta moved in a more radical direction and signed agreements with the Soviet Union, and returned to the newspaper, which went on criticising the government despite threats and forced shutdowns.

From 1987 a group of fourteen parties worked together, and by 1989 Ortega had agreed to free, monitored elections. The National Opposition Union chose Chamorro as its candidate after five rounds of voting. Her platform promised to end the civil war and military service, and she won the election on 25 February 1990 despite polls favouring Ortega.

Chamorro was sworn in on 25 April 1990, the first time in more than five decades that a government had peacefully surrendered power to the opposition. She abolished conscription on the day she took office, cut the army by half to three quarters within weeks and demobilised the Contras. She also granted unconditional amnesties for political crimes. Her administration tackled hyperinflation that had at one point exceeded 13,000 per cent, with a programme of privatisation and a new currency, the córdoba oro.

In 1995 a constitutional crisis arose over reforms that reduced presidential power, which she at first refused to publish. She left office on 10 January 1997, and in July 1997 founded a foundation to support peace initiatives. She moved to Costa Rica in October 2023 and died in San José on 14 June 2025, aged 95.
virgil: Biographical information about Virgil comes chiefly from ancient vitae, or lives, prefixed to commentaries on his work by Probus, Donatus and Servius. The life given by Donatus is thought to reproduce closely a lost life by Suetonius. Some of this evidence relies on allegory and on inferences drawn from his poetry, so details of his life are considered somewhat problematic.

According to the vitae, Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BCE in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, in what is now northern Italy. His ancestry is uncertain, and scholars have proposed Etruscan, Celtic, Venetic, Ligurian or Greek origins. Most sources say his father was an employee of an apparitor named Magius, whose daughter he married. Phocas and Probus give his mother's name as Magia Polla. Confusion between the family name Magius and the noun magus, 'magician', probably contributed to the medieval legend that Virgil was a magician.

The commentators say Virgil began school at five and later went to Cremona, Milan and finally Rome to study rhetoric, medicine and astronomy, which he abandoned for philosophy. His admiring references to Asinius Pollio and Cinna have led scholars to infer that he was for a time associated with the neoteric circle of Catullus. According to the Catalepton, he began to write poetry while in the Epicurean school of Siro in Naples. A group of small works attributed to him by the commentators, the Appendix Vergiliana, is considered spurious by modern scholars, with the possible exception of some short pieces.

The Eclogues are ten poems in dactylic hexameter, roughly modelled on the pastoral poetry of the Hellenistic poet Theocritus. Eclogues 1 and 9 address the land confiscations and their effects on the Italian countryside. Eclogue 4, addressed to Asinius Pollio and called the Messianic Eclogue, uses the imagery of a golden age in connection with the birth of a child whose identity has been debated. Virgil is credited with establishing Arcadia as a poetic ideal. Modern scholars largely reject attempts to draw his biography from the characters of the poems.

His works revolutionised Latin poetry almost from publication, and the Eclogues, Georgics and above all the Aeneid became standard school texts. Ovid parodied the opening of the Aeneid, Lucan wrote an anti-Virgilian epic, and Statius and Silius Italicus engaged closely with him. Servius, a commentator of the 4th century CE, based his work on that of Donatus. Augustine of Hippo confessed that he had wept at reading the death of Dido. In the Divine Comedy Dante presents Virgil as his guide through Hell and most of Purgatory.
virginia: Virginia, officially the Commonwealth of Virginia, lies between the Atlantic coast and the Appalachian Mountains and borders Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, West Virginia and Maryland. Central Virginia lies mostly in the Piedmont, the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, and the Shenandoah Valley holds the state's most productive farmland. Hampton Roads is the site of the region's main seaport and of Naval Station Norfolk.

Hunter-gatherers are estimated to have reached Virginia about 17,000 years ago, and Daugherty's Cave was in regular use as a rock shelter by 9,800 years ago. Farming spread in the late Woodland period, between 500 and 1000 CE. In the 1500s the native population within the present boundaries reached about 50,000. From the 1570s some thirty tribes of Tsenacommacah consolidated under Wahunsenacawh, commonly called Chief Powhatan, forming the Powhatan Confederacy, which governed more than 150 settlements with about 15,000 people in 1607. Three-quarters of the native population died of smallpox and other Old World diseases during that century.

In 1607 the London Company founded the Colony of Virginia, the first permanent English colony in the New World, which gave the state its nickname of the Old Dominion. Enslaved people from Africa and land taken from displaced native peoples fed the plantation economy and also fuelled conflict. The first General Assembly met in July 1619 and is the oldest lawmaking body in North America. Virginians fought in the American Revolution. In the American Civil War the state government in Richmond joined the Confederacy, while many north-western counties stayed loyal to the Union, which led to the separation of West Virginia in 1863.

The capital is Richmond and the most populous city is Virginia Beach; more than a third of the state's people live in Northern Virginia. The 2020 census counted 8,631,393 residents. The state's motto is Sic Semper Tyrannis, Thus Always to Tyrants. Eight Virginians have been President of the United States, including four of the first five, which gave it the name Mother of Presidents. It is governed under its seventh constitution, approved in 1970.
visayas: The Visayas are one of the three principal geographical divisions of the Philippines, along with Luzon and Mindanao. They lie in the central part of the archipelago, mostly around the Visayan Sea, which is also considered the northeast extremity of the Sulu Sea. The region has a land area of 71,503 km2 and consists of seven large and several hundred smaller islands, among them Guimaras, Biliran, Siquijor, Panaon and Bantayan. Palawan, Romblon and Masbate may also be included, since their populations identify as Visayan.

The origin of the name is unknown. A possible first documented use is by the Song-era Chinese maritime official Zhao Rugua, who wrote of the Pi-sho-ye raiding the coasts of Fujian and Penghu in the late 12th century. The Spanish first called the Visayans Pintados, the painted ones, for their full-body tattooing. In his Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas of 1609, Antonio de Morga described them as skilful in navigation and eager for war and raids for plunder, which they called mangubas.

After the Magellan expedition was defeated at the Battle of Mactan by Lapu-Lapu, King Philip II of Spain sent Miguel López de Legazpi to colonise the islands. Many of the local kingdoms began to convert to Christianity, and Spanish and Mexican conquistadors received encomiendas, chiefly on Panay and Cebu; Cristóbal Sánchez, for example, held about 3000 Cebuano tributaries. Resistance followed, including the Tamblot Uprising of 1621 to 1622 and the Bohol Rebellion led by Francisco Dagohoy, which lasted from 1744 to 1829. During the Philippine Revolution the short-lived Federal State of the Visayas took Iloilo City as its capital.

The Visayas are divided into four administrative regions, Western Visayas, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas and the Negros Island Region, with sixteen provinces. Cebu City, Bacolod and Iloilo are among the largest cities. The main languages are Cebuano, Hiligaynon and Waray, with Aklanon, Kinaray-a and Capiznon also widely spoken; Cebuano alone has about 20 million speakers. The Sinulog festival in Cebu City, the Ati-Atihan in Kalibo and the Dinagyang in Iloilo City, all held in January, honour the Santo Niño.
visegrad: Visegrád is a castle town in Pest County, north of Budapest on the right bank of the Danube in the Danube Bend. The name is of Slavic origin and means acropolis, literally upper castle or upper settlement; in Czech and Slovak it is Vyšehrad, and in German Plintenburg. A fortification on Sibrik Hill, just to the north, was built in the first half of the 4th century as part of the Roman frontier along the Danube. The Roman army abandoned it in the early 5th century.

In the 10th and 11th centuries the fortification, rebuilt as a castle, became a regional centre of the new Hungarian state, and the name Visegrád first appears in 1009. The Mongol invasion of 1242 destroyed it, and the town was rebuilt a little to the south, with a new fortification system built by King Béla IV in the 1240s and 1250s. King Charles I made Visegrád the royal seat in 1325.

In 1335 Charles hosted a two-month congress with the Bohemian king, John of Luxembourg, and the Polish king, Casimir III. It was crucial in creating peace between the three kingdoms and an alliance between Poland and Hungary against Habsburg Austria, and another congress followed in 1339. Sigismund moved the royal seat to Buda between 1405 and 1408, and Matthias Corvinus later used Visegrád as a country residence.

The palace was laid out on a square plan of 123 by 123 metres under Louis I and Sigismund, and between 1477 and 1484 Matthias Corvinus had it reconstructed, with Italian Renaissance decoration used for the first time in Europe outside Italy. The Ottomans took Visegrád in 1544, after which the palace fell into ruins and was covered by earth by the 18th century. Excavation began in 1934. The Upper Castle and the Solomon Tower, a hexagonal 13th-century residential tower, are open to visitors.
On 15 February 1991 Václav Havel, Lech Wałęsa and József Antall met there and founded the Visegrád Group, alluding to the meeting of 1335. Visegrád was granted town privileges again in 2000.
visegrad-group: The name refers to the Congress of Visegrád of 1335, where Charles I of Hungary, Casimir III of Poland and John I of Bohemia agreed to create new commercial routes bypassing Vienna, a staple port that required goods to be offered for sale in the city. The congress also confirmed Czech sovereignty over the Duchy of Silesia. A second congress in 1339 decided that if Casimir died without a son, as happened in 1370, Louis I of Hungary, son of Charles I, would become King of Poland.

From the 16th century large parts of the later members' territories came under the Habsburg monarchy, until Austria-Hungary dissolved in 1918. After 1945 the three countries became Soviet satellite states: the Polish People's Republic, the Hungarian People's Republic and the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. Communism fell in central and eastern Europe in 1989.

The group was founded on 15 February 1991 at a meeting in Visegrád of Václav Havel, president of the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic, Lech Wałęsa, president of Poland, and József Antall, prime minister of Hungary. Its aim was to move away from communism and carry out the reforms needed for full membership of Euro-Atlantic institutions such as NATO and the European Union. After Czechoslovakia dissolved in 1993, the Czech Republic and Slovakia became separate members, raising the number from three to four. All four joined the European Union on 1 May 2004, achieving the group's main goal, and the Schengen Area in 2007.

After 2004 the group concentrated on cultural cooperation and on expert-level work on topics such as infrastructure. In 2011 Poland's defence minister announced a Visegrád EU Battlegroup, which stood on standby in 2016, and a patent institute was created by an agreement signed in Bratislava on 26 February 2015.

The International Visegrád Fund is the group's only institutionalised form of cooperation. It supports regional non-governmental initiatives to strengthen ties among people and institutions in Central and Eastern Europe, and Ukraine has been one of its largest recipients. The group has also served as a model: the Craiova Group of Bulgaria, Romania and Serbia, established in 2015, was inspired by it. Its members share a close trading relationship with Germany, particularly in car manufacturing, and the group's networking among public servants and civil society actors has outlasted changes of government.
vishnu: Vishnu is a Rigvedic solar deity, but he does not figure prominently in the Rigveda compared with Indra and Agni: only five of its 1,028 hymns are dedicated to him. Some scholars, among them F. B. J. Kuiper and Jan Gonda, argue that he must have been a more important figure than his infrequent appearances suggest. He rose to prominence in the Brahmana layer of the Vedas in the mid-first millennium BCE. In the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE he was identified with local traditions and deities, particularly the Bhagavata deities Vasudeva-Krishna and Gopala-Krishna and the Pancharatra deity Narayana, and became a divinity of the highest rank, equivalent to the Supreme Being.

Vishnu is the Supreme Being within Vaishnavism and the preserver in the Trimurti, the triad that includes Brahma and Shiva. His name means all pervasive. In Vaishnava belief he creates, protects and transforms the universe, and he is depicted sleeping on the coils of the serpent Shesha in the primeval ocean of milk with his consort Lakshmi. Whenever the world is threatened with evil he descends as an avatar to restore the cosmic order and protect dharma. The Dashavatara are the ten primary avatars, of which Rama and Krishna are the most worshipped.

In iconography he has dark blue, blue-grey or black skin and is usually shown with four arms, wearing jewels. When he descends as Rama and Krishna, Lakshmi appears as Sita and Radha or Rukmini. His mount is the eagle Garuda.

Vishnu is the main subject of the Vaishnava Puranas, of which the most important are the Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu Purana, Nāradeya Purana, Garuda Purana and Vayu Purana. The Tamil Sangam literature, mostly from the early centuries CE, reveres him as Mayon, the dark one. Ideas about Vishnu became important to the Bhakti movement, which swept India after the 12th century. The Alvars, Tamil Vaishnava poet-saints, sang his praises as they travelled and established temple sites such as Srirangam, and their poems were compiled as the Divya Prabhandham.
visigoths: The Visigoths emerged from the Gothic tribes, probably descended from the Thervingi, whose name may mean forest people. Gothic tradition, on which the account of their origins largely rests, places the Goths' beginnings in Scandinavia, with a migration south-east to the Black Sea, though archaeology does not support that legend.

The name Visigoths was apparently coined by the writer Cassiodorus about 507, on the model of Ostrogoths, from the older tribal name Vesi, which is Gothic for good. Until then they were called simply Goths. They spoke an eastern Germanic language that was distinct by the 4th century. They had been Christianized while still outside the empire, but adopted Arianism rather than the Nicene version followed by most Romans, who considered them heretics.

In 376 the Gothic leader Fritigern asked the Eastern Roman Emperor Valens to let his people settle south of the Danube, seeking refuge from the Huns. Famine followed, and the Romans abused the Goths, even forcing them to trade away their children, which led to revolt and six years of plundering in the Balkans.

At the Battle of Adrianople in 378 the Roman army was slaughtered and Valens was killed. Alaric I led the Visigoths from 395. In 397 Arcadius named him military commander of the eastern Illyrian prefecture, and the sack of Rome in 410 followed. In 418 Honorius settled the Visigoths in Gallia Aquitania, where a kingdom grew with its capital at Toulouse, and they later expanded into Hispania.

Defeat by the Franks under Clovis I at the Battle of Vouillé in 507 ended Visigothic rule in Gaul, but the kingdom endured in Spain and Portugal. King Liuvigild (568 to 586) failed to unite Arian and Catholic subjects, and Reccared I converted to Catholicism, a step confirmed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. The kingdom collapsed in 711 after defeat by an Umayyad army at the Battle of Guadalete, where King Roderic was killed.

The Visigothic Code, set in writing in 654 under Chindasuinth, abolished separate laws for Romans and Goths, so that all subjects became hispani, and it protected the property rights of married women. Surviving churches include San Pedro de la Nave, and Reccopolis, founded by Liuvigild to honour his son Reccared, is an archaeological site. The Treasure of Guarrazar, twenty-six votive crowns and gold crosses from the royal workshop in Toledo, shows the high point of Visigothic goldsmithery. After 711 the Kingdom of Asturias arose under Pelagius, marking the start of the Reconquista.
visoko: Visoko lies between Zenica and Sarajevo where the Fojnica joins the Bosna, in a fertile basin ringed by the foothills of the Central Bosnian mountains. The name comes from the Slavic adjective visok, high, and refers to the fortress of Visoki on Visočica hill, first mentioned in a charter of Ban Tvrtko I in 1355. Before that the region around the valley was commonly called simply Bosna, and the settlement below the fortress was known as Podvisoki, below Visoki. Traces of settlement go back to the 5th millennium BCE, and at Okolište one of the largest Neolithic settlements of the Butmir culture in south-eastern Europe was found, with perhaps 3,000 people.

The Daesitiates inhabited the area in antiquity, and the Roman Empire established its rule in 9 CE. The Visoko basin is considered the nucleus of the Bosnian state, which emerged around 1000. Podvisoki, Mile, Biskupići and Moštre together formed the Visoko valley, where many charters were written. Podvisoki, protected by the fortress, was long the main trade centre of medieval Bosnia. At Mile the Rusag, the assembly, met; Tvrtko I was buried there beside his uncle Stjepan II Kotromanić, and Ban Kulin's Plate, dated 1193, was found at Biskupići.

The Ottoman Empire conquered the area around 1463, and the modern town took shape then, its founder being Ajas-beg, a local who had converted to Islam. Up to 1477 he built a hammam, a school, an aqueduct, a bridge over the Bosna, a madrassa and a dervish tekke. Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878. On 11 November 1911 a fire burned down the upper town and the main street, about 450 buildings in all, and rebuilding began in 1912 in brick and tile in a traditional Bosnian style.

Six national monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina stand in Visoko, among them the Old town of Visoki, Mile, the Okolište settlement and the Franciscan monastery of Saint Bonaventure. Šerefudin's White Mosque, by the architect Zlatko Ugljen, received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1983. Visoko has long been known for leather, and before the Bosnian War it was the largest exporter of textiles and leather in socialist Yugoslavia. In 2005 Semir Osmanagić claimed that Visočica and nearby hills concealed pyramids; scientific investigation found no pyramid.
vistula: The Vistula is 1,047 km long and the longest river draining into the Baltic Sea. It rises at Barania Góra in the Silesian Beskids, at 1,220 metres above sea level, and flows through Kraków, Sandomierz, Warsaw, Płock, Toruń, Bydgoszcz and Gdańsk. Near the sea it forms a wide delta, the Żuławy Wiślane, whose channels include the Nogat. Its basin covers 193,960 km2, of which 168,868 km2 lies in Poland. The river took its present shape within the last 14,000 years, after the Scandinavian ice sheet withdrew, and it gives its name to the last glaciation of northern Europe, the Vistulian or Weichselian.
The name first appears in Pomponius Mela in 40 CE and as Vistla in Pliny in 77 CE; Ptolemy wrote Ouistoula. It is often derived from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to ooze or flow slowly.

In the first millennium BCE large parts of the basin were occupied by the Iron Age Lusatian and Przeworsk cultures. Roman authors included the western part among the lands of Magna Germania, and Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE described the river as the border between Germania and Sarmatia. Slavs settled the estuary in the 7th and 8th centuries.

West Slavic Polish tribes formed small dominions from the 8th century, and the ninth-century document of the Bavarian Geographer lists the Vistulans in southern Poland, with Kraków and Wiślica as their main centres. Polish legend ties the river to the beginnings of the state: according to Jan Długosz, Princess Wanda, daughter of King Krak, drowned herself in it rather than marry a German prince.

For centuries the Vistula was one of Poland's main trading arteries, carrying salt, timber, grain and building stone between the 10th and 13th centuries. The Teutonic Knights, invited in 1226 by Konrad I of Masovia, controlled the lower river in the 14th century and captured Gdańsk castle in 1308. In the 15th century Gdańsk became a great centre of trade. Grain shipped on the river rose from 14,000 in 1491 to 310,000 in 1618, and Gdańsk, at the river's end, became the wealthiest and largest centre of crafts in the country.

The river is associated with Polish culture and national identity, flows through the two main cities, Kraków and Warsaw, and gives the phrase Land on the Vistula, which can mean Poland. It is navigable from the Baltic to Bydgoszcz, though navigation upstream is limited. Severe floods over the centuries sometimes depopulated land in the delta, which had to be resettled.
viti-levu: The name Viti Levu means Great Fiji. The island is 146 kilometres long and 106 kilometres wide. Fiji lies in a tectonically complex area between the Australian and Pacific plates, and earthquakes and volcanic eruptions account for the rugged terrain. A mountain range running north to south divides the island into roughly equal halves, and the forested centre includes the nation's highest peak, Mount Tomanivi, also called Mount Victoria, at 1,324 metres. Heavy rain falls on the eastern side, which has Fiji's tropical moist forests. The western side, colloquially called the burning west, lies in the range's rain shadow and is drier, with tropical dry forests and sugar cane.

Viti Levu is believed to have been inhabited longer than Vanua Levu, the island to its north. According to oral tradition, the first Melanesian settlers landed at Vuda Point and founded Viseisei as Fiji's oldest settlement, though archaeological evidence contradicts this account. Many of the ancestors of the Indo-Fijians, who are concentrated in the west, came to the island from India as indentured workers between 1879 and 1916. Indigenous Fijians predominate in the east, except in the cities, which are more mixed.

Viti Levu holds the capital and largest city of Fiji, Suva, and a large majority of the country's people. Other important towns spread along the coast include Ba, Lautoka, Nadi, Nausori, Rakiraki and Sigatoka. Eight of Fiji's fourteen provinces lie on the island. A single major road runs around its perimeter, and Nadi International Airport on the north-west side is the principal airport of Fiji. The island is the only known home of the Giant Fijian long-horned beetle, one of the world's largest insects.
vitoria-espirito-santo: Vitória lies on a small island within a bay where several rivers meet the sea, on the south-eastern coast of Brazil. The municipality of 93 square kilometres has the main island, another 34 islands and a mainland portion; there were originally 50 islands, many of them joined to the largest by landfill. It borders Serra, Cariacica and Vila Velha, and with them forms Greater Vitória. The central massif of the island, Morro da Fonte Grande, rises to 308.8 metres. The climate is tropical, and the city lies in the domain of the Atlantic Forest.

Vila Velha, the first capital of the Captaincy of Espírito Santo, suffered constant attacks from Tupi-Guarani-speaking and possibly some Macro-Jê-speaking indigenous peoples, and from the French and Dutch. The Portuguese therefore chose an island near the mainland, called Guanaani by some of the native peoples. Vila Nova do Espírito Santo was founded there on 8 September 1551 and later renamed Vitória, in memory of a victory won by the captaincy's holder, Vasco Fernandes Coutinho, against the Goytacaz. The city was built on the highlands, which produced narrow streets, and fortresses guarded the exposed lowlands along the coast.

Vitória became a city on 24 February 1823, but its isolation on an island held back its growth. From 1894, during the coffee cycle, landfills in the lower parts changed the shape of the island, new neighbourhoods were settled, public steps joined them to the high ground, old houses were pulled down and sanitation improved. A bridge to the mainland opened in 1927 and the first harbour pier followed in 1941. By 1970 the port ranked among the most important in the country and industrialisation began; the modernisation led to the disappearance of almost all traces of the colonial and imperial periods.

Vitória is the capital of the state of Espírito Santo and the smallest of the 27 Brazilian capitals by area. Its population was 322,869 in 2022, within a metropolitan area of more than 1,880,828. It has two major ports, the Port of Vitória and the Port of Tubarão, and its economy rests on port activity, trade, industry and services, with the steelmaker ArcelorMittal Tubarão and the mining company Vale among its main firms. The Chapel of Santa Luzia, built in the 16th century, is the oldest building in the municipality. The city also administers the islands of Trindade and Martim Vaz, 1,100 kilometres off the coast.
vitus-bering: Vitus Jonassen Bering was born in the Danish port town of Horsens and was baptised in the Lutheran church there on 5 August 1681. His father, Jonas Svendsen, was a customs inspector and churchwarden, and his mother was Anne Pedderdatter. He was named after a maternal great-uncle, Vitus Pedersen Bering, a chronicler at the royal court. The family was reasonably secure financially, and two of his elder half-brothers attended the University of Copenhagen.

Vitus instead signed on as a ship's boy at the age of 15. Between 1696 and 1704 he sailed to India and the Dutch East Indies and completed naval officer training in Amsterdam. He later claimed, with some supporting evidence, to have served on Danish whalers in the North Atlantic and to have visited European colonies in the Caribbean and on the eastern seaboard of North America.

In 1704 Bering enrolled in the navy of Tsar Peter I, where Admiral Cornelius Cruys helped him to a commission as sub-lieutenant. He reached the rank of second captain by 1720. He apparently fought in no sea battles but commanded several vessels on risky missions, and in the last years of the Great Northern War his duties were mostly lightering. On 8 October 1713 he married Anna Christina Pülse at Vyborg; they had nine children, of whom four survived childhood.

Bering was not promoted when the war ended in 1721. After his sister-in-law married a rear-admiral in 1724, he retired to save face, was promoted to first captain on retirement, and rejoined the navy later that year. On 29 December 1724, by the old calendar, Peter I ordered him to lead the First Kamchatka Expedition, to map the lands visited and establish whether Asia and America shared a land border. His lieutenants were Martin Spanberg and Aleksei Chirikov, and the party travelled overland and by river to Okhotsk. He later proposed a more ambitious second expedition, to sail east in search of North America, which involved 600 people at the outset.
vizier: The word vizier is believed to derive from the Arabic wazara, to bear a burden, from the Semitic root W-Z-R. The Quran describes Aaron as the wazir, or helper, of Moses. Proto-Shi'a leaders such as al-Mukhtar and Abu Salama adopted the title wazir al Muhammad, helper of the family of Muhammad. Another view takes it from the Pahlavi vichir, meaning a decree and later a judge, but historians of Islamic administration such as S. D. Goitein reject this and hold the word to be purely Arabic. The Abbasid caliphs gave the title wazir to a minister formerly called katib, or secretary, who had become the representative and successor of the dapir, the official scribe of the Sasanian kings.

The office arose under the first Abbasid caliphs and spread across the Muslim world. The 11th-century legal theorist al-Mawardi distinguished two types: the wazir al-tanfidh, a vizier of execution with limited powers who carried out the caliph's policies, and the far more powerful wazir al-tafwid, with delegated authority over civil and military affairs. The first could be a non-Muslim or even a slave; the second had to be a Muslim well versed in the Shari'a. Women were barred from the office.

In al-Andalus the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba appointed a varying number of viziers as department heads and councillors, as many as 29 at once in 1008, though the senior office was that of the chamberlain, the hajib. The Spanish word alguacil derives from the title. In the Ottoman Empire the Grand Vizier was often the de facto ruling prime minister, second only to the sultan and leader of the Divan, the Imperial Council. Some Ottoman provincial governors, as in Bosnia and Herzegovina, also held the title of vizier.

The title was used for chief ministers in many other states, among them Fatimid Egypt, Muslim Iran, where the prime minister was styled Vazir-e A'zam, the Husainid beylik of Tunisia, the Sultanate of the Maldives, Durrani Afghanistan, and the Bengal Sultanate, as well as by many princes in India. In Tunisia ministers included the Wazir al-Bahr, minister of the sea, and the Wazir al-Qalam, minister of the pen. Wazir remains the standard Arabic word for a government minister, and Waziri is a highly regarded chieftaincy title in much of northern Nigeria, where most emirs have one as a high-ranking adviser.
vlachs: The word Vlach, with many variants such as Wallachian, Vlah and oláh, comes from the name of a Celtic tribe, the Volcae, adopted into Proto-Germanic as *Walhaz, meaning "stranger". In Gothic it came to mean "foreigner" or "Romance-speaker" and later "shepherd" or "nomad". Medieval Romanians called themselves rumân or român, from the Latin romānus, and Aromanians use armãn or rãmãn. Today the term refers chiefly to speakers of Aromanian, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian south of the Danube, in Albania, Bulgaria, northern Greece, North Macedonia and eastern Serbia.

Their origins are disputed. Proponents of Daco-Roman continuity hold that the ancestors of the Vlachs and Romanians descend from Dacians and survived in the lower Danube basin in the Migration Period. The other theory holds that Romanians and Vlachs were one group of Eastern Romance speakers whose origins lie in the southern Balkans, with early Romanian speakers moving north from the 12th century.

In medieval sources Vlach was an exonym, and it could also refer to other peoples, so it ranked, in the words of the Serbian historian Sima Ćirković, with names such as Greek, Serb or Latin. In 976 Vlachs fought and killed David of Bulgaria between Prespa and Kastoria. Around 1000 they were present in large numbers on the Chalcidice peninsula, where they were known for cheese and meat products. In 1020 the Archdiocese of Ohrid was founded with responsibility for the spiritual care of all the Vlachs, and in 1027 many Vlachs recruited from Macedonia served in the Byzantine army that tried to recapture Sicily.

Between 1105 and 1109 correspondence between Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and Patriarch Nicholas III Kyrdiniates mentions 300 Vlach families serving the monks of Mount Athos, who were expelled after the patriarch complained about their pasturing. The traveller Benjamin of Tudela was one of the first to use the word for a Romance-speaking people, placing them in the mountains of Thessaly. In 1330 Stefan Dečanski gave Vlach pastures and katuns along the Drim and Lim rivers to the Visoki Dečani monastery. Transhumant pastoralism took hold only between the 14th and the 19th centuries.

Vlach shepherds drove flocks through the mountains of central and eastern Europe, and groups were found as far north as Poland and Moravia and as far west as Dalmatia, where Slavs called them Vlasi or Valaši. As national states appeared in the area of the former Ottoman Empire, new borders divided the summer and winter habitats of many transhumant groups. Ilona Czamańska notes that research on Vlach origins was long dominated by political issues. Some researchers have also raised concern about the denial of Vlach descent of various groups and personalities.
vlad-the-impaler: Vlad was the second legitimate son of Vlad II Dracul, who took his nickname from membership of the Order of the Dragon, a fraternity founded by Sigismund of Luxemburg, King of Hungary, to halt the Ottoman advance. Dracula is the Slavonic genitive, meaning the son of Dracul. In modern Romanian dracul means the devil, which added to his reputation.

The historian Radu Florescu writes that Vlad was born in Sighișoara, where his father lived from 1431 to 1435. In 1442 Vlad and his younger brother Radu were held as hostages in the Ottoman Empire to secure their father's loyalty. In 1447 his father and eldest brother Mircea were murdered after John Hunyadi invaded Wallachia and installed Vladislav II as voivode.

Vlad took Wallachia briefly with Ottoman support in October 1448, but Vladislav returned and Vlad fled by 7 December. After exile in Moldavia and Hungary he invaded Wallachia with Hungarian support in 1456, and Vladislav died during the invasion. Vlad purged the boyars and came into conflict with the Transylvanian Saxons, whose villages he plundered, impaling the captives, which gave him his epithet.

When Mehmed II demanded personal homage, Vlad had the sultan's two envoys captured and impaled. In January 1462 he attacked Ottoman territory, massacring tens of thousands of Turks and Muslim Bulgarians. He tried to capture the sultan at Târgoviște on the night of 16 to 17 June 1462. The Ottomans withdrew, but many Wallachians deserted to Radu.

In late 1462 Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, had Vlad captured. To justify this to Pope Pius II and the Venetians he produced letters said to be Vlad's, which most historians regard as forged. Vlad was held at Visegrád from 1463 to 1475 and released at the request of Stephen III of Moldavia. He was reputedly made to convert to Roman Catholicism. After fighting with Corvinus's army in Bosnia, he regained Wallachia in his last attempt to hold the throne, but Basarab Laiotă returned with Ottoman support. Vlad was killed in battle near Snagov before 10 January 1477.

Stories of his cruelty circulated in his lifetime, and courtiers of Corvinus promoted them after his arrest. The poet Michael Beheim wrote a poem about him that was performed at the court of Emperor Frederick III in 1463, and such books were among the first bestsellers in German-speaking lands. Some in his region regarded him as a folk hero for opposing the Ottomans. His name is linked to Bram Stoker's vampire Count Dracula of 1897, although Stoker's notes do not name Vlad directly. Stoker learned of vampires from Emily Gerard's article on Transylvanian superstitions, published in 1885. Tursun Beg called him Kazıklı Voyvoda, the Impaler Lord.
vladikavkaz: Vladikavkaz is the capital of North Ossetia-Alania in Russia. It lies in the south-east of the republic at the foothills of the Caucasus, on the Terek River. The Russian name literally means "ruler of the Caucasus", while the Ossetian name Dzæudžyqæu means "Dzaug's settlement". The Soviet period gave it other names: in 1931 it was renamed Ordzhonikidze after the Soviet leader Sergo Ordzhonikidze, who established Soviet power in the region during the Civil War; in 1944, after the deportation of the Chechens and Ingush, it became Dzaudzhikau; in 1954 it was Ordzhonikidze again. In 1990 it took the double name Vladikavkaz in Russian and Dzaudzhikau in Ossetian.

The city was founded in 1784 as a Russian fortress at the entrance to the Darial Gorge, to serve as an outpost on the routes between Russia and Georgia. Accounts differ on the site: it is said to stand near the Ingush village of Zaur, while many other sources place it on the Ossetian village of Kapkai. The Georgian Military Highway, linking it with Georgia across the mountains, was built in 1799, and a railway connected it to Rostov-on-Don and Baku in 1875. Under the Russian Empire it was the administrative seat of the Vladikavkazsky Okrug of the Terek Oblast.

It was the capital of the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which existed from 1921 to 1924 and covered most of modern Chechnya, North Ossetia and Kabardino-Balkaria. In February 1919 the anti-Communist Volunteer Army under General Anton Denikin seized the city, and the Red Army expelled it in March 1920. In early November 1942 German forces tried unsuccessfully to take it and left North Ossetia in January 1943.

Vladikavkaz is one of the most populous cities of the North Caucasus. It is an industrial and transport centre producing processed zinc and lead, machinery, chemicals, clothing and food. Trams have run since 1904. The Mukhtarov Mosque, built in 1906, dominates the city, and the Georgian Military Road begins there. Most residents are Eastern Orthodox, with a minority following Sunni Islam and followers of the Ossetian folk religion Uatsdin.
vladimir-ii-monomakh: Vladimir was the son of Vsevolod Yaroslavich, who reigned as Grand Prince Vsevolod I of Kiev from 1078 to 1093. In 1046 Vsevolod had made a diplomatic marriage to a relative of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, from whom Vladimir probably took his nickname Monomakh. The Primary Chronicle names his mother only as a Greek princess. A later story that he defeated Constantine and was given the name in a peace settlement is impossible, since the emperor died in 1055. The name first appears in a eulogy in the Kievan Chronicle and on his seal.

As a young prince Monomakh ruled in Smolensk and Chernigov and led 13 campaigns in the name of his father. In 1068 he allied himself with the Cuman chief Bilge-Tegin. After 1094 his chief patrimony was Pereyaslav, though he also controlled Rostov, Suzdal and other northern provinces, where he founded several towns, notably the one named Vladimir. His quarrel with his cousin Oleg began when Oleg made peace with the Polovtsians to retake Chernigov, and it continued among their descendants.

Monomakh initiated three princely congresses, at Lyubech in 1097, Vytachiv in 1100 and Dolobsk in 1103, to unite the princes against the steppe by allowing each princely branch to keep its patrimony. Between 1103 and 1111 the Rus princes raided the Polovtsians every year. In 1107 Monomakh defeated the Cuman khan Boniak, and in 1111, with Sviatopolk II, he led the army that defeated a Cuman force at the river Salnitsa, probably near modern Izium. These victories drew the Cumans into the steppes and prevented new raids. His Instruction states that he conducted 83 campaigns and made peace with the Polovtsians 19 times.

When Sviatopolk II died in 1113, the people of Kiev revolted, attacking officials, wealthy citizens and Jews. The ruling circles invited Monomakh, the most liked prince, to take the throne. He lowered the rate of interest on loans and issued decrees that prohibited usury, banned the enslavement of merchants indebted through accident, regulated the status of bondsmen and restricted the power of the boyars.

His statute was included in the revised Russkaya Pravda. He wrote his Instruction to Children about 1117, a didactic and autobiographical work that condemns princely strife and promotes the idea of a unified state. He was buried in Saint Sophia Cathedral. Later generations remembered his reign as a golden age, before Rus was torn apart by internal struggles after the death of his son Mstislav in 1132.
vladimir-lenin: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov was born in Simbirsk on 22 April 1870 (10 April O.S.), the third of eight children. His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, came from a family of former serfs and rose to be Director of Public Schools for the province, a post that carried hereditary nobility. Lenin took up revolutionary socialist politics after his brother's execution in 1887 and was expelled from Kazan Imperial University for protesting against the Tsarist government. In late 1893 he moved to Saint Petersburg and rose to a senior position in a Marxist cell. Arrested for sedition in 1897, he argued in prison that industrial capitalism had created a proletariat that would overthrow Tsarism. He was exiled to Siberia, where he married Nadezhda Krupskaya.

In 1903 Lenin took a key part in the split of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and led the Bolshevik faction. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he campaigned for the First World War to be turned into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. He returned to Russia after the February Revolution of 1917 and helped lead the October Revolution, in which the Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government.

His government at first shared power with the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917 gave the Bolsheviks about a quarter of the vote; it met in January 1918 and was forcibly disbanded. By 1919 Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries had been expelled from the soviets and Russia was a one-party state. The government redistributed land, nationalised banks and large industry, left the First World War by a treaty conceding territory, and won the Russian Civil War. Opponents were suppressed in the Red Terror, in which tens of thousands were killed or interned. In 1921 Lenin encouraged economic growth through the New Economic Policy.

Lenin fell seriously ill in 1921, suffered strokes in May and December 1922, and died at Gorki on 21 January 1924. Joseph Stalin succeeded him as the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government. His interpretation of Marxism, first called Leninism by Martov in 1904, became the basis of Marxism-Leninism and a model for later Communist-led states. Supporters see him as a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism, while critics accuse him of establishing a totalitarian dictatorship that carried out mass killings and political repression.
vladimir-mayakovsky: Vladimir Vladimirovich Mayakovsky was born on 19 July 1893 in Baghdati, in the Kutais Governorate of Georgia, then part of the Russian Empire. His father, a local forester, belonged to a noble family. At home the family spoke Russian, but with friends and at school Mayakovsky spoke Georgian. At fourteen he took part in socialist demonstrations. His father died suddenly in 1906, and his widowed mother moved the family to Moscow.

In December 1912 his first published poems appeared in the Futurist manifesto A Slap in the Face of Public Taste, signed with Velemir Khlebnikov, David Burlyuk and Alexey Kruchenykh, which called for throwing Pushkin, Dostoyevsky and Tolstoy off the steamboat of modernity. In December 1913 the Futurists toured 17 cities in riotous readings that police often stopped; the tour cost Mayakovsky and Burlyuk their places at the Art school. He met Osip and Lilya Brik in July 1915 and recited A Cloud in Trousers to them, dedicating it to Lilya.

During the Russian Civil War he produced agitprop posters for the Communist Party, and he edited the art journal LEF. His work showed support for the Bolsheviks and admiration for Lenin, but his relationship with the Soviet state was complex. Works that satirised it, such as the plays The Bedbug and The Bathhouse of 1929, met with scorn from the state and literary establishment.

Futurism rejected traditional poetry in favour of formal experiment and welcomed the social change promised by modern technology. Mayakovsky's verses of 1913, with words split into pieces and staggered across the page and peppered with street language, were considered unpoetic. His idea was to create a democratic language of the streets. A Cloud in Trousers of 1915 treated love, revolution, religion and art from the viewpoint of a spurned lover.

He died on 14 April 1930 by his own hand, and about 150,000 people attended his funeral. After his death his publications were cancelled for a time, until Joseph Stalin wrote in 1935 that he was the best and most talented poet of the Soviet epoch.
